Brian Greene said: “as particles … try to move through space, they have to burrow through the Higgs field, and that is what gives them mass”. Does that mean that particles that keep at rest in the frame of the Higgs fied are gravitationally massless? Brian Greene’s “explanation” is one of many popularizations of physics that are intended to make difficult topics accessible to the “unwashed masses” but in reality, achieve the exact opposite. I would put it in the same basket in which I put the “rubber sheet” analogy of gravity, the “expanding balloon” description of cosmic expansion, even the “miniature solar system” models of the atom. Then I would put that basket out onto the curbside for collection. No, particles do not “burrow through” anything. If they “burrowed” through anything, that would mean a loss of kinetic energy through dissipative processes. Soon enough, everything would come to a halt, floating in some sticky molasses I suppose… But no, I swear, that is not how the Higgs works. Remember that mass is energy? No, mass is not “converted” into energy or vice versa. What we call inertial mass, or rest mass, is the internal energy-content of a thing. That’s what E = m c 2 is about, not about nuclear energy or converting anything into anything: It literally tells you that mass and (internal) energy are the same thing. Equivalent. Unsurprisingly, the equation itself is called the mass-energy equivalence relationship. In the Standard Model of particle physics, most particles start off as massless particles, but they interact with the Higgs field. However, the Higgs field has a very peculiar property. In empty space (i.e., the lowest energy state achievable, the vacuum) the Higgs field itself is not “empty”, so to speak. So particles can interact with it even when there’s supposedly nothing there. In effect, particles interact with the vacuum. Interaction means potential energy. (E.g., when two objects interact by, say, repelling one another, you need to invest energy to push them together, and that energy will be “stored” as their interaction energy while they are close to each other.) When an initially massless electron, for instance, interacts with the vacuum, it means it carries that interaction energy with it, no matter what it does or where it goes. And because the vacuum is everywhere, so to speak, the electron cannot get rid of that interaction energy. It’s always there. That interaction energy shows up, for all practical intents and purposes, as part of the energy-content of that electron. And as I stated above, energy-content means inertial mass. So the electron behaves as a massive particle, because no matter where it goes, what it does, it carries along that interaction energy with the vacuum Higgs field (to be more precise, the so-called vacuum expectation value, or v.e.v., of the Higgs field). So I stress, no “burrowing” is involved. The Higgs field has no rest frame, and how fast or how slow the particle moves with respect to this non-existent rest frame is irrelevant. In its own reference frame, a particle is always at rest. But it still has inertial mass, because the potential energy of its interaction with the Higgs field is there, no matter what.

How does a black hole destroy matter but not light? It doesn’t destroy either. Not right away anyhow. From the outside, a black hole is a massive, very compact thing. Its gravity is very strong when you are near it, but you have to get really, really close. From afar, its gravity is exactly the same as the gravity of any other object of the same mass. If we were to replace the Sun with a black hole of the same mass, we’d no longer have sunlight of course, but the Earth would continue in the exact same orbit as before. When you approach the Sun, even if you could withstand the heat, you cannot get any closer than about 700,000 km from its center, because at that distance, you’d run into the Sun’s surface. A black hole of the same mass has a radius of a mere 3 km. So you can get more than 200,000 times closer to its center and still be “outside”. Since the gravitational force is proportional to the inverse square of distance, this close to the black hole the gravitational force is more than 40,000,000,000 times stronger than the gravitational force at the surface of the Sun. But, I stress, this extreme gravitational force requires getting really close to the black hole, just over 3 km! At 700,000 km, the gravity of a black hole with the same mass as the Sun is exactly the same as the gravity of the Sun 700,000 km from its center (i.e., at the solar surface); at 150,000,000 km (the Sun-Earth distance) the black hole’s gravity is the same as the Sun’s at this distance, which is why it’d keep the Earth in the same orbit. When something gets too close to the black hole, the black hole’s strong gravity means that it can no longer escape. Whether it is a particle of matter or a ray of light makes no difference. No escape means no escape. As to what happens to things that do get too close: once inside the event horizon of the black hole, it’s game over. The “interior” is like a mini-universe: it contains all the things that ever fell, ever will fall, into the black hole. But unlike our “outside” universe, this mini-universe is in a state of collapse. The time it takes may range from milliseconds to hours, depending on the size of the black hole, but it’s finite, very finite indeed. And once it’s over, it’s over, for matter and light alike. Time itself ends inside the black hole. But this is not something we ever see from the outside. Gravitation means time dilation (clocks slowing down). Extreme gravitation means extreme time dilation. As viewed from the outside, time dilation becomes truly extreme indeed near a black hole’s horizon; no matter how long we watch, we can never see things reach the horizon or the horizon to form. Things would disappear from sight (due to gravitational redshift, any signal becomes weak and undetectable) but no horizon is ever seen. For this reason, in some of the older/foreign literature, black holes had another name: “frozen stars”. So there: far from destroying either matter or light, as seen from the outside black holes appear to be doing the exact opposite: “freezing” all infalling stuff forever! How is the speed of gravity determined? First of all, while I recognize that this is a bit of semantics, there is no “speed of gravity” any more than there is a “speed of electromagnetism”. Gravity is an interaction, it does not have an inherent speed. However, influences in the gravitational field, far from sources, travel as transverse waves, and these indeed do have a speed. Theory tells us that this speed is the same as the speed of influences in the electromagnetic field, i.e., electromagnetic waves such as light. While few had real doubts that this prediction is valid, its first observational test came seven years ago with the LIGO event GW170817. This gravitational wave event turned out to be the collision and merger of a pair of neutron stars, an event that was also detectable in a multitude of electromagnetic frequencies. The electromagnetic and gravitational signals arrived at the same time, even though they event took place some 130 million light years from here. This tells us that indeed, gravitational and electromagnetic waves traveled at the same speed. As a matter of fact, this had a direct impact on theory. There are proposed alternative theories of gravitation in which there is not one but two (or more) metrical fields, one determining the speed of gravitational waves, the other, the speed of electromagnetic waves. These “bimetric” theories were essentially falsified by the GW170817 observation.

How can virtual particles become real particles e.g. while Hawking radiation? I suspect that this question was at least inspired by the popular, but fundamentally misleading “explanation” that Hawking radiation is about the creation of virtual particle-antiparticle pairs near the horizon, one of which is swallowed by the horizon, while the other is released as a “real” particle. This explanation, though it first appeared I believe in Hawking’s own popular science book, is nonetheless nonsensical, in direct contradiction with Hawking’s own 1974 paper (Nature 248 (5443)), which explains how gravitational vacuum polarization, along with the past-future asymmetry of a system in a perpetual state of collapse, leads to a net outgoing radiation. But I suspect there is also a misunderstanding here concerning the nature of particles, be they real or virtual, in the context of quantum field theory. Take the electromagnetic field. The classical theory is Maxwell’s: it’s a field theory, which is to say, it describes something that is present everywhere, with a continuously varying value from point to point in space and time. This field may be sourced by electric charges. If charges are absent, the field equations can still have nonzero solutions, which are in the form of plane waves traveling at constant velocity (the velocity that we know as the vacuum speed of light). When it comes to the quantum theory, we start with decomposing the field into elementary frequencies, kind of like how a sound can be decomposed into elementary pure sounds of different pitch. Each of these pure waves can be treated as a “harmonic oscillator”, which, in the quantum theory, has discrete levels of energy. It is these discrete levels, or packets, of energy that will be the field quanta, and it is these quanta that we perceive, under the right circumstances, as particles. When we write down the equations of fields, especially interacting fields, the equations include nasty summations (integrals) of ever more complicated interactions. As a mental aid, however, we can think of these interactions in terms of one unit, one quantum at a time, and even use neat little diagrams (the Feynman diagrams) as a bookkeeping device, keeping track of these terms. The arrows in that Feynman diagram are suggestive of particle-like behavior. Even though no actual particles are involved, it can sometimes be helpful to intuit these interactions as exchanges of “virtual particles”. Unfortunately intuition in particle physics is a dangerous business. Helpful, yes, but do not forget for a moment that these are merely bookkeeping devices. There are no miniature cannonballs, virtual or otherwise. Only interacting fields. The “particle” aspect is entirely imaginary, existing only in our heads, as a clumsy mental aid to help our limited intuition. That’s what “virtual” really means.

I’m having a bit of trouble understanding how to visualize elementary particles as waves but doing the photon/gluon/virtual particle interaction processes. I do not understand why antimatter is visually necessary in field animations. Why? You stumbled upon the most fundamental aspect of quantum physics: You cannot visualize or intuit it. I mean it. No, it’s not some ivory tower mentality telling the lowly masses that they are too dumb. I mean… you see, here is a good example. I am sure you, like almost everyone else, tried GPT or one of its cousins. It is striking just how capable these language models are, yet sometimes, they fail even on relatively simple tasks. Why? Because they cannot visualize anything. They simply lack the hardware, the senses, the training data. GPT can only think in terms of words, not in terms of shapes, diagrams, visuals. We humans can. Why? Because our brain has the hardware. But it’s hardware with limitations. Specifically, the parts of our brain that can do “intuitive” models are capable of modeling a classical, nonrelativistic, three-dimensional universe. Quantum physics does not fit in. It not only cannot be visualized, any attempt to do so actually stands in the way of understanding. Now just like GPT, we can still learn about these things and make inferences. But not by intuiting them. Rather, by using disciplined deductive reasoning, employing the precise language of mathematics. It is hard, of course, just as hard as it is for GPT to reason about the spatial relationships between objects using only the power of words. But it’s the only way. Going back to the subject of the question. The first step is that elementary… .things are neither particles (miniature cannonballs) nor waves in the classical sense. Rather, the mathematical steps basically go like this: We write down the (classical) equations of motion; we do some algebra, re-expressing everything in terms of the state of the system; and then we turn the equation on its head, asking what other states of the system would work. These new solutions make absolutely no sense in the classical world. The electron is neither a miniature cannonball nor a wave: however, it no longer even has a definite position. (Or, if you wish, it’s in many places at once.) Not only that, but the theory is fundamentally nonlocal: Some of the conserved quantities, for instance, that constrain a system cannot be tied to any particular spot in space or time, but constrain the system as a whole. In a quantum particle theory, that electron may interact with an instrument and exhibit classical properties like a specific position: a “particle”. Yet when we describe the state of the system, that state is characterized by a mathematical entity that is a wave solution, a wavefunction, which can be used to compute probabilities of the electron showing up here or there. But the electron is neither that particle-like flash in a detector, nor that wavefunction determining probabilities. The best that we can say is that an electron may exhibit wave-like and particle-like behavior both; but it is neither a wave nor a particle. So what is it, then? To answer that, we need to go beyond a quantum particle theory. But first: a quantum particle theory can also be used to describe a system that is called a harmonic oscillator, well known from classical physics. In quantum physics it acquires a peculiar property: Its energy levels are discrete, “quantized”. This is important. So then, going beyond the particle theory: Meet fields, things that exist everywhere, characterized by values that are assigned to every point in space and every location in time. How can we deal with a field in a quantum theory? Well, we can decompose a field into a sum of harmonic oscillators, a bunch of sine waves. (NOTHING to do with the wavefunction I mentioned above.) Why would we do that? Because each of those harmonic oscillators can be quantized. And now the field’s behavior can be characterized by those harmonic oscillators bumping up or bumping down by one unit of energy at a time. Lo and behold, these can correspond to the creation and annihilation of particles! The equations can get nasty at this point when we try to describe interacting fields. We get some awkward integrals. They can be “tamed” sometimes by expanding them into series and keeping track of ever smaller terms in a summation. Every one of these terms can be conceptualized as an exchange of excitations, i.e., “particles”. They really aren’t particles. But using the concept of a “virtual” particle, which really is just a mathematical tool, we can keep track of these terms. Keep this in mind. Virtual particles are not visualization tools. They are bookkeeping tools, keeping track of terms in a mathematical sum. As to why antimatter is needed, that depends on the specifics of the field involved. Some fields describe particles and corresponding antiparticles. Other fields describe only one type of particle that may serve as its own antiparticle in interactions. In any case, it’s not about any “visual” necessity. It’s simply the nature of the solution, the nature of the theory, whether antiparticles are predicted by it or not. Ultimately of course the theory must agree with experiment. Electrons have antiparticles; photons don’t (they’re their own antiparticles, in a manner of speaking). The theory accurately reflects the nature of both. OK, this answer became longer than I anticipated, so here’s the most important take-home lesson: Do not try to intuit or visualize the quantum world. Any attempt to do so creates an obstacle to understanding. If you seek real, in-depth understanding, unfortunately the math cannot, must not, be avoided as it is the only tool that the human brain has at its disposal to understand something this far removed from our sensory experience. According to relativity, gravity slows time (time dilation) and causes length contraction? Does Dark Energy, which is accelerating the expansion of the Universe, speed time and cause lengthening is space? OK, it doesn't exactly work that way. Gravity doesn't slow time, speed time, or change lengths. However, according to the theory of RELATIVITY (never forget the name!) observers in different gravitational fields will measure things differently. So what takes 1 second according to the clock of an observer in a strong gravitational field may take 2 seconds according to the clock of an observer in a weak gravitational field. This of course implies that we have a spatially varying gravitational field, which changes from point to point. Cosmological models are usually homogeneous models: that is, they assume that on average, the gravitational field is the same everywhere, it only changes with time. Over time it becomes weaker in an expanding cosmos, because matter flies apart and becomes less dense. When dark energy is present, stuff flies apart faster. And the rate at which it flies apart decreases more slowly. The Hubble parameter, rather than going down to zero as matter becomes less and less dense, settles down on a nonzero value instead. Expansion continues. As a result of that expansion, there is redshift. Some of it is just plain old velocity-related Doppler, due to things flying apart. But some of it (over cosmological scales, especially) is due to the time-varying gravitational field. On average, matter is less dense today than yesterday, so its overall gravity is weaker today than yesterday, so clocks today appear to tick faster than clocks yesterday. A signal emitted billions of years ago at a certain number of oscillations per second will show fewer oscillations per second as measured by a clock today. Dark energy does not fundamentally change this, but it alters the rate at which cosmological parameters, including the redshift, evolve over time. How is mass not conserved when it's literally E^2-p^2, and both quantities are conserved? The equation, m 2 = ( E / c 2 ) 2 − ( p / c ) 2 , or simpler yet, using units such that c = 1 , m 2 = E 2 − p 2 , indeed describes the invariant rest mass of an isolated particle. However, it does not imply that rest mass is conserved in interactions. As a simple example, consider the collision of an electron and a positron. In the center-of-mass reference frame, their three-dimensional momenta are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction: p e = − p p where I used p to represent the 3-dimensional momentum vector. And of course both the electron and the positron have the same invariant rest mass m e . So before the collision, we have m 2 e = E 2 e − p 2 e , m 2 e = E 2 p − p 2 p , for the respective particles, from which we can also conclude that E e = E p = E (i.e., I dropped the superfluous index), so the total energy of the system is 2 E . The total momentum of the system is, of course p e + p p = 0 according to the rules of vector addition, and the total rest mass 2 m e . The collision annihilates the electron-positron pair, producing (usually) two photons. Energy and momentum are conserved. That means that the momenta of the two photons must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so their vector sum is zero. And the total energy of the two photons is 2 E . This implies that each photon has energy E with a corresponding momentum of p = E / c in magnitude, pointing in opposite directions for the two photons. The rest mass, however, is now zero. As an aside, I would like to mention two more thoughts, not directly pertinent to what I just demonstrated, but food for thought, nonetheless. First of all, this reasoning can also inform you right away why an electron-positron pair cannot annihilate into a single photon. In the center-of-mass reference frame, the net momentum must be zero, both before and after; but the energy is nonzero. If the result of the annihilation was a single photon, it would have zero momentum but nonzero energy, which is not possible. Second, now that I demonstrated that the sum of rest masses is not invariant, allow me to offer a twist of the story. Imagine this whole thing took place inside a closed box. Both before and after, the respective particles (the electron-positron pair before the annihilation, the photons after) interact with the walls of the box that keep them confined. Well, guess what: the rest mass of the total system (measured, e.g., by measuring the force that is required to accelerate the box at a certain rate) remains unchanged throughout the process. Which is just a demonstration of the rather important point: namely that the rest mass of a system is equivalent to its internal energy-content. It does not matter what form that energy is in: kinetic energy, potential energy, even the rest masses of constituent bits. The rest mass of the box is the total internal energy of the box material and everything it encloses.

Is there empirical evidence against John Moffat's modified gravity (MOG), also known as Scalar-Tensor-Vector-Gravity (STVG)? Disclaimer: I have worked with John Moffat so my views may not be impartial. The essence of Moffat’s gravity is that metrical gravity is stronger than it would be in general relativity; however, this is canceled out by a repulsive force due to a vector field interaction of finite range. For a galaxy, this means that in its inner region (where cancelation due to the vector field is present) the behavior is Newtonian; farther from the center, galaxies rotate faster because the vector repulsion is now absent and thus, gravity is stronger. The coupling parameter that governs the strength of these interactions, and the mass parameter that governs the range of the vector force are both scalar fields (perhaps the same scalar field in disguise), so the values vary from system to system. As a result, the theory can do away with the need for dark matter. Dark energy may or may not have to stay. A key feature of the theory, which distinguishes it perhaps from families of modified gravity theories that offer behavior consistent with MOND (Modified Newtonian Dynamics) is that whereas MOND-like theories are governed by a fixed acceleration scale, MOG is governed by scales determined by the mass, and distance from, the source. MOG survives many observational tests. In the solar system, treating the Sun as a single source, the parameters of the theory have negligible values so we get general relativity at the post-Newtonian level. Multimessenger observations (neutron star mergers observed using both electromagnetic and gravitational waves) are consistent with MOG as, unlike many other theories, MOG only has one metric which implies that electromagnetic and gravitational radiation propagate at the same speed. MOG is also consistent with the apparent Newtonian behavior of massive but compact galaxies, as well as the Newtonian behavior of wide binaries. And MOG may actually work well, better even than the standard cosmological model, when it comes to colliding galaxy clusters, including the famed Bullet Cluster that was supposed to be a slam dunk case in favor of standard cosmology, but also clusters that challenge the standard model. And MOG is at least approximately consistent with large-scale cosmological observations, including the large-scale distribution of matter and the cosmic microwave background (though some problems remain). Personally, I find that the biggest challenge (which can make or break the theory) is to find a consistent analytic formulation for the scalar fields’ mass dependence in the weak field limit. This has not been done yet; we have semianalytic formulas that associate values for these parameters with compact sources, but that’s the best we’ve been able to derive. Resolving this question, along with addressing the assumption that MOG, despite the presence of the vector force, satisfies the weak equivalence principle (which kind of implies that perhaps there is a metrical formulation of the theory) are issues that I consider vey important but frustratingly difficult to tackle properly.

Is it true that everything travels at a constant velocity in deep space, near the speed of light? No, it is not true. First of all, in the context of relativity theory, it is important to remember that the concept of speed is relative. Things do not travel at some velocity, nor do that stay put. Things travel relative to other things. To give you an example that dates back to Galileo: Suppose you are on a sailing ship, sitting in a windowless cabin as the ship sails on perfectly smooth seas. You are staring at a glass on the table in front of you. The glass is not moving. Or is it? How could you even tell? Relative to you, the glass is at rest. Relative to the shore, it moves at some velocity (how fast do medieval sailing ships move anyway?) along with you and the table and the rest of the ship. But relative to the Sun? It moves about 30 kilometers every second! Or how about relative to the central region of the Milky Way? We’re now up to roughly 200 km/s. And then relative to some really distant objects in deep space, you, your glass and the table it sits own, your ship, the Earth, the Sun, the Milky Way all move at a speed close to the vacuum speed of light. And it goes both ways. From your perspective, it’s not you or the Earth that is moving so fast, but the distant galaxy! However, if there are aliens on that galaxy, they’d say it’s you who is moving and they’re the ones standing still. So as I said, motion is relative. And constant it is not. If there were no forces (including gravity) acting on objects, motion (relative as it is) would always be in a straight line at constant velocity. But there are forces. Gravity in particular (a force that we often interpret geometrically) alters the trajectories of objects. So they no longer move in a straight line or at a constant speed relative to other things. The Earth moves around the Sun, and its Sun-relative velocity changes in magnitude, too, as its orbit is elliptical. The velocity of the Earth relative to, say, Mars, is even more twisted. These specific examples notwithstanding if there is one thing that is worth remembering, it’s that velocity is always relative. That applies even to light in a vacuum. The magnitude of its velocity is the same for all observers, but the direction in which a light ray travels is different in different observer reference frames. (In fact, if you look up the concept of aberration in astronomy, this has been known since before relativity theory, for over 300 years as a matter of fact).

Isn’t it true that the general theory of relativity suggests the existence of black holes, white holes, negative value e=mc2 energy, wormholes, quantum entanglement, cosmological, constant gravitational waves, and a host of other amazing things? No. General relativity does not “suggest” any of the above. General relativity provides one thing: a set of equations that govern the behavior of the gravitational field. That’s it. End of story. R μ ν − 1 2 R g μ ν = 8 π G T μ ν . That is all. This equation has many solutions, just like Maxwell’s equations for the electromagnetic field have many solutions. Just because something is a solution of the field equations of a theory does not mean that this solution represents physical reality. Solutions for equations like this one are constrained by conditions. These could be “boundary conditions” (e.g., the expectation that the field vanishes large distances from a source). These could be symmetry conditions (e.g., the expectation that a compact mass has a spherical gravitational field that does not depend on time.) These expectations narrow down the range of solutions. So let’s pick apart the specific points listed in the question. Well, I hope my answer puts those questions into a proper perspective. We can be impressed by the magnificence of Nature and be grateful for our ability in these modern times to actually make sense of some of it without turning explanations into science-fiction fairy tales. What is the cause of a black hole's immense strength? How is it possible for something to have infinite density and gravity? A black hole does not have immense strength or infinite density. Mostly, no infinite gravity either. Take a black hole that has the same mass as the Sun. Put it in place of the Sun. Guess what happens to the Earth? Apart from the lack of sunlight (which would be bad news for us humans) absolutely nothing. The gravity of that black hole is exactly the same, finite gravity as that of the Sun. Density? Sure, a stellar sized black hole is dense. Actual black holes do not form at a mass much less than about three times the mass of the Sun. But even neutron stars are insanely dense, many trillions of times denser than water. But… this may come as a surprise but very, very large black holes are not so dense at all! When we talk about the largest supermassive black holes, they can form at densities less than the density of ordinary water. It’s only when the black hole is relatively small (by that, I mean, three times the mass of the Sun, which would be “only” a million times the mass of the Earth) that such insane densities are encountered as matter collapses into a black hole. And then, the gravity. As I said, at the same distance as the Sun, a one solar mass black hole has the same gravity as the Sun. Far from infinite. So let’s get a little closer. In the case of the Sun, the closest we can get to its center is about 700,000 kilometers, before we collide with the Sun’s surface. At that distance, solar gravity is powerful (about 30 times the gravity of the Earth at sea level) but far from infinite. And you cannot get any closer, because now you would be inside the Sun. But now take that black hole. A black hole with the same mass as the Sun has an effective radius of only about 3 kilometers. Going from 700,000 to 3… as you know, gravitational acceleration is proportional to the inverse square of distance. So now we are up to trillions of times Earth gravity! And that’s just the Newtonian result. Once we take relativity theory into account, there is, after all, one infinity to deal with. At exactly the event horizon, you would literally need an infinitely powerful rocket exerting an infinite force to hover. But that’s because the event horizon has this strange spacetime geometry: “hovering” means the same thing as moving at the vacuum speed of light. Which, as we know, is not possible without an infinitely powerful rocket. But anywhere outside the event horizon, gravity is finite. And it’s strong not because the black hole’s gravity is stronger than the gravity of another object of the same mass, but simply because you can get that much closer to it. As another example, take the Earth. Its radius is roughly 6,370 kilometers or just under 4,000 miles. The radius of a black hole of the same mass? Less than 9 millimeters. Just over one third of an inch. Imagine something with a diameter of two thirds of an inch, not larger than what one of my cats would produce when he is constipated, a pebble really, that weighs as much as the entire planet Earth. Why is graviton difficult to detect? Do we have any good reasons to believe it exits in the first place? The graviton is difficult to detect because gravity is very weak, which means that the probability of any particular graviton to interact with matter is very, very, very low. The late Freeman Dyson in his 2012 Poincaré Prize lecture calculated that the Sun, in addition to the humongous amount of thermal energy it emits as electromagnetic radiation (mostly light), also emits about 79 megawatts of thermal gravitational radiation. Now 79 megawatts is not a lot for a star, but it is certainly a respectable amount: For comparison, we’ve been able to reliably detect a mere 8 watts in the form of a radio signal from the Pioneer 10 spacecraft when it was roughly 80 times farther from the Earth than the Sun. So Dyson calculated what it would take to detect a single graviton event, i.e., an atomic transition caused by a captured graviton, from this radiation, using the entire Earth as a perfect graviton detector. His result: We’d see roughly one graviton every billion years. That is how weakly gravity interacts with matter. Concerning the second half of the question, no, we do not “believe” that gravitons exist. Belief is done in other places. Rather, we know that if the gravitational field is a quantum field much like electromagnetism, in the so-called perturbative limit (basically, when the field is weak) it would manifest itself in the form of discrete quanta, which we call gravitons. So detecting gravitons would confirm our suspicion that gravitation, too, is a quantum phenomenon. Conversely, if we had a firm prediction that gravitons should be detected in a given experiment, and we failed to see those gravitons, that would at the very least falsify the idea that gravity is similar a a quantum field theory to electromagnetism. (Perhaps it is still a quantum theory, but something manifestly different.) The trouble is, we can do neither. We can neither detect gravitons nor reliably exclude their existence based on observations that we can do. So we end up speculating. There are plenty of theories out there, both quantum theories of gravitation and alternatives. Some are better than others, but we really have no way to decide which is right: without experiment, without observation, we are blind, and although we are reasonably clever monkeys, at no time in the history of science were we able to figure out something like this on our own, without hints from Nature as far as I know. Do electromagnetic waves have momentum? If so, do waves and sound waves have momentum? Yes, electromagnetic waves have both energy and momentum. When an object emits some light in a specific direction, it is pushed backwards ever so slightly. Similarly, when an object absorbs or reflects light, it is pushed by that light. (Experimental spacecraft with solar sails use the momentum of sunlight to accelerate.) As to sound waves, you can even visualize it. A sound wave is a pressure wave. Recall what happens when a very loud sound wave hits, say, a window pane. The glass shatters. It shatters because of the force (change in momentum) as momentum from the incoming sound wave is transferred to the glass. So yes, sound waves also carry momentum. As do waves in general. What is the origin of the energy resulting in an explosion during the merger of two neutron stars that do not result in a black hole? Black hole, no black hole, the energy is there, the end result doesn’t matter much. At first it is gravitational potential energy: the “ability to do work”, i.e., bring things into motion. When the two stars are far apart but attracted to each other, as they get closer, they speed up. So potential energy “does work”, gets converted into kinetic energy. A good chunk of that kinetic energy is radiated away in the form of gravitational radiation as the two stars orbit each other in an ever tighter inspiral, reaching a substantial fraction of the vacuum speed of light towards the end. But then, kaboom, they collide. That means that whatever kinetic energy they have left (which is to say, stupendous amounts of kinetic energy when an entire star moves at a sizable percentage of the speed of light) is now converted into heat. Think of a large meteorite impact… and now multiply that by, I don’t know, maybe a 30-digit number. So if the end product is not a black hole, what we have instead is an object that is heated to insane high temperatures as a result. (This also becomes a factory for heavy elements. Chances are your own body contains quite a few atoms that were produced in such a collision.) As a matter of fact, more energy is released by the impact if the end result is not a black hole, as all that heat can radiate away, instead of being gobbled up by the resulting black hole. But in the end, it’s just plain old gravitational potential energy, converted into motion (kinetic energy) and, upon impact, into more random motion (heat). Nothing fancy, really, apart from the sizes and scales involved. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Is there any way, other than throwing some mass in the opposite direction, to move forward in space? To move forward in space, you don’t need to do anything. Once a body is in motion, it remains in motion unless a force acts upon it… and in space, no such forces are usually present. However, if you want to accelerate a body, things change. Acceleration means a change in the body’s momentum. But momentum is one of those quantities that are always strictly conserved. So if you change the momentum of a body, the momentum of something else, somewhere, must change by an equal but opposite amount. Reaction mass could be that something else. This is how rockets work. However, if you find something outside of your space vehicle, perhaps you can change its momentum without throwing anything away. For instance, here in the vicinity of the Earth, you might be able to interact with the Earth’s magnetic field and accelerate; in exchange, the Earth itself would accelerate in the opposite direction, but given how much more massive the Earth is compared to a spaceship, this change in the Earth’s momentum is imperceptible. It might be possible to repeat the feat on larger scales, using, e.g., the magnetic field of the Sun or even galactic magnetic fields, albeit these fields are very weak so the sheer size of whatever equipment might accomplish this miracle likely makes the concept impractical. It is also possible to make use of the momentum of something already there, e.g., sunlight. Or the momentum of something we put there ourselves, e.g., light from a powerful ground-based laser. In both cases, the spacecraft would have a lightsail that, as it interacts with (and changes the momentum of) the light it receives, imparts a momentum on the spaceship that carries it. There is also gravitational assist: When there are at least two bodies in a system (and there are certainly more than two bodies here in the solar system) it is possible to follow a trajectory that changes direction with respect to one of the bodies, but changes direction and magnitude of velocity with respect to the other. Again, momentum is conserved: the motion of the bodies involved also changes. But again, bodies such as planets in the solar system are so much heavier than a spaceship, any change in their momenta will remain imperceptible. Throughout it all, however, the common theme is that books must always remain balanced when it comes to momentum. If your spaceship accelerates in some direction, something else — propulsion mass, a planet, rays of light, whatever — must accelerate in the opposite direction. What if when your at the singularity of a black hole (if there is one), looking back out to space may look like a singularity also? Can that be? Ok-kay… when you are “at the singularity” of a black hole, your world has come to an end. The singularity is not a place you can be at, but a time: specifically, for anything unfortunate enough to have crossed the event horizon of a (Schwarzschild) black hole, it is an unavoidable moment in time in the near future. In case you are wondering what you might see after you crossed the event horizon but before your world ends at the singularity: no, you cannot “look back”. Not without a time machine. Like the singularity, the event horizon is also a moment in time: a moment in time in your past now. Your present is characterized by an environment that can be mathematically described by the same equations as a collapsing mini-universe. (You may not be a “comoving observer” so the mini-universe might have a skewed appearance, so to speak, but that makes no real difference.) This mini-universe is collapsing and there’s nothing you can do about it, just as there’s nothing you can do, here and now, tou avoid encountering 8 AM tomorrow a few hours from now. So no, you cannot look back. Now whether or not it is even possible to reach an event horizon or if it perhaps evaporates first, or whether or not a black hole with even a small amount of rotation might look materially different “inside” from the Schwarzschild case… I don’t know, and I don’t think anyone has an unambiguous answer, since Hawking evaporation remains a semiclassical model, and as for spinning black holes, no one constructed yet a fully convincing model of what a collapsing, spinning cloud of matter does beyond the horizon. But we do know how things work in the case of a non-spinning Schwarzschild black hole: There is no looking back. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

If a light ray of white light is bent by the gravity of a massive object like a star, does the light ray undergo diffraction and turn into a rainbow? No, it does not, and that is a very important point. The refractive index of transparent materials tends to depend on wavelength. That is to say, light rays of different color will travel at different speeds in that material, and therefore follow different paths. This is why a lens, a prism can split a white ray of light into its constituent colors, creating a rainbow pattern. Gravitational lensing is different, and this has to do fundamentally with the weak equivalence principle. Gravitation is an “equal opportunity” interaction: It does not care about the material properties of the thing that is affected by it. Two rays of light following identical trajectories will be deflected by an identical amount, regardless of their color. This would not be the case, mind you, if the speed of light itself depended on wavelength. And that would be the case if light was a result of an interaction mediated by a particle with mass. But electromagnetism, the interaction behind light, is not mediated by a massive particle. It is mediated by photons, which are massless, so always travel at the vacuum speed of light regardless of their kinetic energy (which in turn determines their frequency, i.e., their color.) So red light and blue light, for instance, despite being substantially different in terms of the energy of the individual photons, will follow the same path in a gravitational field. Having said all that, it is still possible for a gravitational field to produce a rainbow-like effect, but for a different reason. Here is an example of a simulated projection by a gravitational lens with that is not perfectly spherical (i.e., it has a quadrupole mass moment), of light from a point source onto a projection surface: The reason why the colors of the rainbow appear in this image is not because the gravitational lens affected light of different color differently. Rather, it has to do with the constructive/destructive interference of the light wavefront as it arrives at the projection surface; the peaks and valleys of this interference pattern are wavelength-dependent, so we see, e.g., red peaks vs. blue peaks at different locations. Is Newton's conception of gravity as incompatible with Einstein's concept of gravity, as Einstein's is from the quantum? How, or how not? None of the above incompatibilities are true. First, Newton himself knew that his gravitational theory is incomplete. It involved “action at a distance” between celestial bodies, with no means, no medium to mediate that interaction. To quote the man himself (letter to Bentley, Feb 25, 1692/93): "That gravity should be innate inherent & {essential} to matter so that one body may act upon another at a distance through a vacuum without the mediation of any thing else by & through which their action or force {may} be conveyed from one to another is to me so great an absurdity that I beleive no man who has in philosophical matters any competent faculty of thinking can ever fall into it. Gravity must be caused by an agent {acting} consta{ntl}y according to certain laws, but whether this agent be material or immaterial is a question I have left to the consideration of my readers." Einstein completed this theory, though by no means was he the first to try. In the wake of the success of Maxwell’s theory, especially after special relativity made it clear that the electromagnetic field is a fundamental entity, not just waves of some medium (the luminiferous aether), many sought a similar field theory of gravitation. It took a while to understand why a scalar theory would not work, and why a tensor theory necessarily doubles as the observed geometry of spacetime. Einstein succeeded, and by doing so, ultimately answered the riddle posed by Newton more than two centuries earlier. And of course Einstein’s theory yields precisely Newton’s in the weak field, nonrelativistic limit. General relativity is a classical field theory. It is not fundamentally incompatible with quantum physics. We can do quantum field theory on the curved background of general relativity. (Indeed, popular topics such as Hawking radiation arise precisely as a result of such an approach). We can even have quantum matter act as the source of classical gravitation, in the form of semiclassical gravity. We find this unsatisfactory, however, in much the same way Newton was not satisfied with his own theory of gravitation: We sense that it is not the final word on the subject and further improvements are needed. But we would expect such an improved theory to yield Einstein’s in the semiclassical limit, and yield Newton’s in the semiclassical, nonrelativistic limit. No incompatibilities there, just gradual improvements in our understanding, one step at a time. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Can anything emerge in space other than mass and energy to be equivalent and convertible to mass or energy? If it can then how will we write E=mc2? You don’t “convert” things into mass or energy. Mass or energy do not have an independent existence. Energy is a property of a thing. Any thing has intrinsic energy-content, in addition to its motional (kinetic) energy, which, in turn, depends on who is looking: If I travel with you on a train and you are not moving relative to me, you have zero kinetic energy in my reference frame, but a substantial amount of kinetic energy in the reference frame of the station. Intrinsic energy-content is, well, all the kinetic energy (e.g., thermal motion) and potential energy (e.g., binding energy holding molecules, atoms, elementary particles together) in a body. The energy-content of a body is its inertial (rest) mass. As to E = m c 2 , contrary to countless bad popularizations, it has nothing, absolutely nothing (!!!) to do with converting anything into anything else. This expression is called the mass-energy equivalence (not “conversion”) relationship, and it is the mathematical expression of the statement that I made above: an object’s inertia, its rest mass, is its internal energy-content. The factor of c 2 exists only because it is the natural conversion factor between units of energy and units of mass; in so-called “natural units”, c = 1 anyway, and the expression is simply E = m . Why does general relativity predict that the wavelength of light will be shifted due to the galaxies mass in an effect called gravitational redshift? Relativity theory predicts two things that can result in redshift: Clocks in a gravitational field tick slower than clocks in empty space. Consider a light source that produces green light at a frequency of 6 trillion cycles a second. Suppose this light source is in a strong gravitational field. You observe it and measure that indeed, the light source produces 6 trillion cycles a second according to a clock right next to it. But then you measure that light using an instrument in deep space. The light appears yellow. You measure it and it's comes in at only 5 trillion cycles per second according to a clock next to your receiver. Even though the two clocks (the one in the deep gravitational well and the one in deep space) are identical, flawless clocks they will tick at different rates. For ever 6 ticks of the clock in deep space, the clock in the gravitational field will tick only 5 times. As that clock counts to 5, the source emits 30 trillion cycles. The clock in deep space will count six times as those 30 trillion cycles arrive. Now the funny business is that the speed of that light will be measured both at the source and at the detector at 300,000 km/s. Fewer cycles means longer wavelength, then. So the same light that appears to leave the source with a wavelength of 500 nm (that is to say, 500 nanometers between emitted cycles) will be measured at 600 nm between cycles at the receiver in deep space. This is gravitational redshift. Now this example assumed that the locations are stationary. What if they aren't? If the distance between the light source and detector decreases, each subsequent cycle will arrive a little sooner as it had less distance to travel. Conversely, if the distance increases, each subsequent cycle takes a tad longer to arrive. So this, too, can change the number of cycles that are received over a unit of time. This is the Doppler frequency shift (redshift if the distance between source and detector is increasing). Perhaps you were thinking about cosmology. Relativity theory also predicts another important thing: In the cosmos, on the largest of scales, matter is not at rest. Things are either flying apart or coming together (that is to say, the matter density of the cosmos is either decreasing or increasing over time). In our cosmos, things appear to be flying apart. When things are flying apart, the distance between them increases over time. So there is a Doppler redshift. But as the density of matter decreases over time, so does its average gravity. So if light traveled for a long, long time it's coming from a distant past when the gravitational field was stronger so clocks were ticking more slowly compared to the present. So there is also a gravitational component to this cosmic redshift. The Doppler part dominates for relatively nearby galaxies; the gravitational part, for very distant stuff. To stress, I am not talking about the individual galaxy's own gravitational field that can cause a small amount of redshift; I am talking about the overall average gravitational field (i.e., the average magnitude, say, of the curvature scalar, to be a tad technical) that changes over time as the matter density of the cosmos decreases. Why does the weakness of gravity prevent scientists from finding the graviton? We detect particles by detecting their interactions with other particles. The strength (or weakness) of the coupling between the particles determines the “cross-section”, basically the likelihood, that a detectable interaction occurs. When the coupling is really, really weak, such interactions occur very rarely. In a 2012 lecture[1], the late Freeman Dyson presented an interesting calculation. The Sun, on account of being hot, emits not only thermal electromagnetic radiation but also thermal gravitational radiation. The same blackbody spectrum, just gravitons, not photons. Sure, gravity is very weak compared to electromagnetism, so instead of the several hundred septillion watts that it emits in the electromagnetic spectrum, the Sun “only” emits about 79 megawatts of thermal gravitational radiation, but that is still a respectable radiating power. If we had a 79 megawatt light bulb at 1 astronomical unit (the Sun-Earth distance) from here, we’d have no trouble detecting it, and no trouble detecting individual photon events from that source using a suitable detector. But this 79 megawatts is not in the form of electromagnetic waves but in the form of gravitational waves. Now Dyson imagined using the entire Earth, every last bit of it, as kind of a “perfect” graviton detector: That is, he assumed that we can somehow monitor the entire Earth in a completely noise-free setting, and detect a single atomic transition (an electron jumping to a higher orbit) as a result of capturing a graviton. I.e., direct detection of a graviton, much the same way we can detect photons with a suitable detector. The result: Dyson’s calculation told us that we would see, on average, one such graviton event every billion years or so. That is what it means to have a very weak coupling between the gravitational field and matter. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

If we accept that dark matter exist, they must be part of the entire planet Earth, including living plant and animal organisms. In this case, is it correct to believe that dark matter is part of the human organism? If dark matter exists, it is indeed presumed to be present everywhere, though its density is very low compared to terrestrial densities. However, I’d hesitate to call it a “part of”, e.g., organisms. By way of an example that is known to exist with certainty, right now there are countless neutrinos going through your body. Are they part of your body? Not really. Why? Because neutrinos are effectively non-interacting. To them, your body might as well not be there. And vice versa, for your body the presence of the neutrinos makes no difference. Neutrinos still interact with ordinary matter though, just very, very, very weakly. An awful lot of neutrinos would be needed to make a noticeable difference. Sure, if you happened to be situated near an exploding supernova, the neutrino flux might be enough to evaporate you in an instant, but for that, the explosion of an entire giant star would be required, fairly close to you. In contrast, the millions, billions, trillions of neutrinos that pass through your body right this moment make no difference whatsoever. They are not part of you. The presumed dark matter of cosmology interacts even less with ordinary matter. So even if it is present right here, right now, it is not part of you, of animals, plants, or the Earth. It happens to be in the same place in space at the same time, but it might as well be in another galaxy far, far away: There is no interaction, no connection between that dark matter medium and your body. So no, whether or not dark matter exists remains to be seen, but it is definitely not part of the human body. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Was the German mathematician Hilbert's final derivation of the general relativity found to contain a key error by subsequent peer scholars? So Einstein is still regarded as the first person to publish the correct equations of general relativity? I think it was a bit more nuanced than that. Einstein and Hilbert corresponded frequently in 1915, as they were both working on the problem of finding the field equations of gravitation. Einstein was trying to discover the field equations more or less heuristically. He was not concerned with the nature of matter. He left the stress-energy tensor essentially unconstrained other than its basic symmetry properties. His theory was a theory of gravitation, not matter. Hilbert, on the other hand, inspired in part by earlier work by Mie, was more specific. His stress-energy tensor was intended to be representative of what we today would call a classical "theory of everything", encompassing electromagnetic fields and matter. The two corrresponding frequently in November 1915. Based on what we know (see, e.g., Abraham Pais's scientific biography of Einstein), I think it is fair to say that the physical theory of general relativity is undeniably Einstein's (Hilbert himself referred to this as Einstein's theory.) It seems likely that they both discovered the field equations independently, though undoubtedly, they both benefited from their frequent correspondence. Hilbert deserves credit for showing us the way to derive the field equations of gravitation from an action principle, as opposed to just postulating them like Einstein did. It should be stressed perhaps that by late 1915, the goal was in sight and the nature of the theory that Einstein sought was clearly understood. The missing bit? It seemed clear that the gravitational field is represented by the contracted Riemann curvature tensor, i.e., the Ricci-tensor R μ ν . However, the Ricci tensor does not have the symmetry properties associated with the stress-energy tensor of matter, which is to say, the Ricci-tensor is not divergence-free. The key final step in formulating the field equations is the inclusion of the − 1 2 R g μ ν term in the field equations. This term would follow from Hilbert's action, but based on, e.g., surviving galley proofs, it appears that this final form was not yet present in Hilbert's initial draft, only in later (1916) revisions. (See also General relativity priority dispute - Wikipedia for some details.) Hilbert's "mistake" if it can be called that is that he was perhaps too ambitious: Using Mie's work, he was trying to construct "the foundations of physics" (the explicit title of his paper). In contrast, Einstein was focusing on "the field equations of gravitation" (that was the actual title he used). Hilbert's original approach, as explained by Pais, also contained mistakes not related to the specific form of the field equations. Further, Pais suggests (and he’s probably right) that although the two men corresponded frequently, they pursued very different approaches and different goals, and may have “talked past each other”, neither paying sufficient attention to absorb the approach of the other. Today, we call the tensor G μ ν = R μ ν − 1 2 R g μ ν the Einstein tensor; the field equations of gravitation are the Einstein equations; however, the action integral from which these field equations can be derived, S = ∫ d 4 x √ − g ( 1 2 κ R + L m a t t e r ) is called the Einstein-Hilbert action. Einstein and Hilbert had a bit of a dispute but their later correspondence remains friendly. The reason for the dispute probably had nothing to do with the actual discoveries in late November 1915, and may have had something to do with Einstein feeling that Hilbert plagiarized some ideas he presented in a talk (again, according to Pais). What is the propagator for a massless scalar field, and how can you compute it using C++? The propagator for a massless scalar field, which obeys the Klein-Gordon equation ∂ μ ∂ μ ϕ = 0 , can be derived from the Green’s function of this equation, ∂ μ ∂ μ G ( x − y ) = δ 4 ( x − y ) that, in momentum space, becomes − k 2 ~ G ( k ) = − 1 , hence ~ G ( k ) = 1 k 2 + i ϵ , where we introduced a small imaginary term, as usual, to avoid the singularity at k = 0. By itself, this expression is not something you would compute numerically in a language such as C++. You may be able to derive expressions of this sort in computer algebra (either general purpose CAS with specialized packages or special purpose systems). The propagator is used in combination with the vertex rules of a theory to compute cross-sections corresponding to particle interactions. That computation itself may not be trivial as it involves divergent integrals that may need to be regularized in order to obtain meaningful results for observable quantities. In short, no, unless you first use C++ to build a CAS for quantum field theory, you would not be using C++ for this type of computation. You might use a CAS to derive an expression for an observable quantity that you then import into a C++ program for numerical evaluation (perhaps as part of a larger computation) but the propagator on its own is not something you’d likely use in C++. Does the existence of Hawking radiation suggest that nothing truly enters a black hole? It might. The jury is still out, given that Hawking radiation represents an approximate solution to a rather tough family of problems. But first things first. Black holes, first and foremost, are mathematical abstractions. That is to say, they are neat mathematical solutions to Einstein’s field equations, but as we know thanks to Oppenheimer and Snyder’s landmark 1939 paper and many other studies on the subject since, we know that the black hole is the “asymptotic end state” of gravitational collapse. In other words, a black hole is what an outside observer would see after waiting an infinite amount of time. At any finite time, no matter how far into the future, the observer would see “continued contraction” (an expression used in the title of the Oppenheimer-Snyder paper), subject to ever greater time dilation, never ending, never reaching the end state characterized by an event horizon. An infalling observer, however, would supposedly reach the event horizon after a finite amount of measured (proper) time. The horizon, for this observer, is a moment in time: once it is reached, there is no going back, as a return to the horizon would necessitate time travel to the past. That’s the classical picture. Now enter quantum field theory, in a so-called semiclassical approximation. First of all, forget that neat but fundamentally incorrect depiction of particles and antiparticles created near the horizon, one with positive, one with negative energy, with the latter swallowed by the black hole. Yes, this depiction comes straight from Hawking’s book, even though it contradicts his own 1974 landmark paper that reveals the true nature of Hawking radiation. It has to do with collapse. Namely that a black hole is, as Oppenheimer-Snyder told us, in a state of continued contraction. This means that the past and the future are not symmetric. Express this statement in the language of quantum field theory, in the presence of the strong gravitational field of the collapsing object and presto: you get outgoing radiation. The characteristic wavelength of that radiation is roughly 20 times the Schwarzschild radius of the black hole that is yet to be formed. The consequence of Hawking radiation is that the energy-content of the collapsing object evaporates in finite time. A very, very long time to be sure, but finite. This statement seems to suggest that in this case, no event horizon ever forms in the first place. It is indeed my inclination to jump to that conclusion but I need to be careful. The semiclassical picture if fraught with traps for the unwary. We treat gravity in this scenario as entirely classical, ignoring any possible contributions from quantum gravity. And of course part of the problem is that all this is the kind of physics that may remain forever untestable. To create an experiment, we’d need to create black holes which requires several times more mass than the mass of our entire solar system. Then we’d have to wait an unimaginably long number of years, typically characterized by a 70-digit number, give or take, before the evaporation completes. Throughout most of this time, Hawking radiation is so incredibly weak, no conceivable instrument, present or future, can detect it. (Don’t be mislead by breathless pronouncements of laboratory “black holes”: these are analogous experiments that, at best, replicate some superficial aspects of black holes.) What would happen if something went through a black hole? What would happen if something went through a black hole? Well, I’d say it’d be proof that time travel exists, and perhaps the television series Dr. Who is not a science-fiction show but a documentary. You see, the event horizon of a black hole is not something that is here, now, which you can go “through”. The event horizon of a black hole is a moment in time. In fact, so long as you are outside of that event horizon, it forever remains a future moment in time. And if you reach the horizon to get “inside” the black hole, the horizon becomes a past moment in time for you. So to go “through” a black hole (which is to say, enter the black hole and then re-emerge, in the finite future of any outside observer), you’d have to travel backwards in time. Kind of hard to do without a time machine like the aforementioned Dr. Who’s fames TARDIS.

Is it really true when the action lab said that if negative mass exists, it would chase a positive mass and the positive mass would repel accelerating until it sped up faster than the speed of light? First of all, negative mass almost certainly does not exist in this universe. Be thankful that it doesn’t: If it did, its mass-energy content being less than zero, it would allow the vacuum to decay into negative mass particles, implying that our entire universe is unstable, subject to collapse. Not exactly a desirable prospect. Having said that, if negative mass did exist, then, at least in the context of classical (be it relativistic or nonrelativistic) gravitational theory, it would indeed repeal everything; however, it would still be attracted to positive masses. The result would be as you describe: If we had, say, a device with a negative and a positive mass of equal magnitude, the positive mass would be pushed by the negative mass, but the negative mass would be pulled by the positive mass, so there would be an unceasing net acceleration. And no, it would not violate conservation laws either, since the total mass of this particular system would be zero, hence its kinetic energy and momentum would also be zero. But no, not even this system would speed up beyond the vacuum speed of light. As viewed by a distant observer, its acceleration would bring it ever closer to the vacuum speed of light but never quite reaching it. It would behave just like the classic Internet physics FAQ example of the relativistic rocket under constant acceleration. Long story short, negative mass may have the power to destroy our universe through eternal quantum collapse, but it still does not have the power to alter the basic principles of relativity theory.
