For a long-duration moon mission, would an Earth-corrected time standard be required, or would periodic corrections to Earth time be sufficient? It depends on what you want to achieve. As others noted, gravitational time dilation amounts to a roughly 60 microsecond difference per day. If you are only interested in making sure that you don’t miss your favorite TV show, you have nothing to worry about for at least a good half century, which is when the cumulative difference reaches about a second. But as they say, the devil is in the details[1]. What are you using your clocks for? If you are doing navigation using precise radio signals, GPS-like, then keep in mind that every microsecond amounts to about 300 meters when it comes to straightforward length measurements; depending on the geometry of the problem, when you are looking at satellites at an angle, the navigational errors can quickly add up to several kilometers. Needless to say, when you’re landing a spacecraft, several kilometers might mean the difference between a nice, flat region vs. the boulder-filled interior of a nasty lunar crater. Not good! Moreover, while it is true that the time dilation averages to about 60 microseconds a day, it is highly variable. The rate at which clocks tick on the Moon relative to terrestrial clocks (or clocks in intermediate orbits around the Earth, like GPS clocks) depends on many factors other than lunar gravity, including the gravity of the Earth itself, the gravitational field of the Sun (the Moon may be closer to, or farther from the Sun than the Earth at various points during a lunar orbit, and this affects relative clock rates) not to mention the relative motion of the respective clocks. Ultimately it is still a simple problem (just account for all the sources of gravitational time dilation and add them all up — nonlinear effects can likely be safely ignored as they are many orders of magnitude smaller) but it still requires making sure that everything is properly accounted for at the requisite level of accuracy. Long story short, my expectation is that before long, there will be a lunar reference time standard, likely as a result of some international agreement. Future missions, including missions that might be used to assist navigation in cislunar space, will probably use that standard. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Can I buy a quantum computer? Are they real, or are they just news wanting views? Well, yes… but no. Allow me to explain. Or rather, allow me to begin my answer with a question: What do we call a “quantum computer”? Because the definitions, unfortunately, shift depending on who is offering the announcement of the day about yet another breakthrough, yet another declaration of “quantum supremacy”, or let’s face it, yet another request for research grants. So if money is no object, what can you buy that others might call a “quantum computer”? Well, you can certainly buy an experimental device that has a couple of qubits (the basic unit characterizing the capabilities of a quantum computer). You may get one for a few thousand dollars. Not very useful or practical, mind you, just an educational toy. If you have a lot more money, you can also buy a system (or more likely, have one custom-built for you) with more qubits, but apart from the sticker shock, be prepared for the need to set up a special facility to host, and support, the hardware. And in the end it, too, would amount to little more than an expensive educational toy, with no practical utility whatsoever. Or you can buy a system like D-wave’s quantum annealer, which is basically an analog computer that is particularly suitable for certain classes of optimization problems. But it is not a general purpose quantum computer. Which leads me to the answer I’d like to offer to my own question: a true, general purpose quantum computer is a scalable quantum computing machine. One that has as many qubits as I need, one that can be expanded with more qubits if necessary. This is not something that you can buy no matter how much dough you have, because it is not something that exists today, and may never exist in the future. Some compare the current state of quantum computing to the dawn of digital computers. But that is a false comparison. Sure, the Intel 4004 CPU was very primitive compared to its present-day counterparts. But the architecture was scalable. I could, in principle, build a circuit with a thousand 4004 CPUs. I could use bank switching and attach gigabytes of memory to a single 4004 CPU. Sure it would be damn inconvenient, cumbersome and very costly, but the system would work. There is no underlying physics principle that prohibits the existence of a million-CPU supercomputer with a terabyte of RAM, based on the 4004. It would be a darn stupid thing to build, but it can exist. This is not the case with quantum computing. You cannot add qubits galore, no matter how much money you have. The culprit is fundamental physics: the famous threshold theorem, in particular. The promise of general-purpose quantum computing is based on this theorem. You see, quantum computers are based on the premise that even though qubits have only two states when they are read, during the operation of the quantum computer it’s not those two states but their superposition, characterized by a continuous quantity (e.g., the phase of the wavefunction), that interacts with similar qubits in the system. The problem is that the qubits are not only entangled with each other, they also tend to get entangled with everything else in the universe. We try to keep the qubits as isolated from the environment as possible, to prevent environmental decoherence. This isolation is necessarily imperfect. But here is where the threshold theorem kicks in: If we can keep this decoherence below a certain threshold, there exist error correction algorithms that allow a system of qubits to emulate a perfect quantum computer with fewer qubits. The trouble is, this threshold has so far proven elusive. All those machines that I mentioned above, including cheaper commercially available units or pricier research installations? None of them are scalable. None of them beat the threshold theorem. Can the theorem be beaten? An entire industry, billions of dollars are wagered on that possibility. I am in a skeptical minority: I think it will prove to be a no-go theorem. Of course it is very possible that I am wrong. But until I see a credible announcement of a quantum computer architecture that beats the threshold theorem, my skepticism remains. So then, the answer to your question is that, well, yes, you can buy systems that are called “quantum computers” and they are not deceptive, you just need to know exactly what it is that they are selling. But no, you cannot buy a true, scalable general-purpose quantum computer because no such thing exists today.

Is it sexist that women are not being selected to win a Nobel Prize? Could it be that the work of those women do not measure to the actual work the winners of the awards have accomplished? Here's a quote from a recent video by Sabine Hossenfelder: [...] I wasn’t offered a job because I’m a woman. I'm not guessing that that’s what happened, I know, because they told me. You see, the guy who was head of the institute told me that, since I'm female I should apply for a scholarship that was exclusively for women in the natural sciences. Because then the institute wouldn't have to pay for me. I met Sabine (at the Perimeter Institute). My impression was that she radiated self-confident knowledge and competence. To the extent I am qualified to judge, she came across as a very sensible, good physicist with a well-earned reputation, who has put a lot on the table in her career as a professional physicist, and who would never pull the “gender card” to complain. The situation she describes sounds awfully familiar, probably repeated far too often at universities and research institutes around the world, even today. Women face a multitude of obstacles, starting with the cultural: the “hard” sciences are often presented as male pursuits, whereas women should supposedly be more interested in, I don’t know, arts, crafts, or raising babies. I suspect that this already discourages far too many talented young women. Then there is human biology: the birth of a child can burden any parent, but the burden is obviously disproportionately the mother’s, starting with pregnancy and childbirth itself. Family expectations may pile on top of cultural stereotypes: The young mother may be expected to stay at home with the children, while the father assumes the traditional role of breadwinner. Obstacles like that which Sabine encountered may not even be based on downright gender prejudice. Institutions may simply be worried that hiring a woman is like playing the lottery: The woman may get pregnant, perhaps multiple times, absent from her position for extended periods of time. But yes, old-fashioned, ugly gender prejudice is likely still present at times, not to mention unacceptable behavior like harassment or worse. I recall a discussion I once had with someone, about Sabine: the person I was conversing with questioned her competence, unfavorably comparing her to a much younger (male, of course) physicist who has not yet published anything notable at the time. It was clear to me that I was witnessing an outburst of classic, old-fashioned sexism. And it doesn’t take much to change the statistic. When you look at Nobel laureates, they represent an extreme, one of the trailing ends of the Gaussian curve characterizing the scientific community. All it takes is a small shift of the curve to the left, barely noticeable in its central part, for there to be an order-of-magnitude difference near the trailing ends. In short, even if I boldly assume that we no longer need to worry about gender bias in the Nobel selection process that may have deprived the likes of Lise Meitner, Emmy Noether, Cecilia Payne, Jocelyn Bell Burnell, Vera Rubin or Chien-Shiung Wu, just to name a few examples (if the names are unfamiliar, look them up, it’s worth your time), of well-deserved recognition, the cards are still far too often stacked against women by both biology and society. Writing this reminded me of one of my heroes, a person who surely would have deserved a Nobel prize, if only computer scientists qualified for one. I am of course talking about the amazing Grace Hopper, mathematician, computer scientist, and rear admiral of the United States Navy, at the time of her retirement the oldest serving commissioned officer in the armed forces of the United States. One of the things she is known for may not be universally liked but it is still widely in use today, nearly 65 years after its invention: The COBOL programming language.

Were the space shuttles capable of aborting a descent from orbit and re-establishing that orbit? That might have saved the Columbia shuttle if it were possible. No, unfortunately that’s not the way it works. Let’s do a teeny bit of math. What do you think requires more energy? To lift a spacecraft to an altitude of around 400 kilometers, where the ISS orbits, or to accelerate the spacecraft to orbital speed? Well, the gravitational potential energy can be estimated crudely using E = m g h . Let’s just use g = 10  m / s 2 , and we get about 4  M J for every kilogram of spacecraft. Kinetic energy, in turn, is E = 1 2 m v 2 , and orbital speed is roughly 8  k m / s . So that would be roughly 32  M J . In other words, almost 90% of the energy spent to launch that shuttle was used to accelerate it, not to lift it. Now about that re-entry. It begins with a small burn that alters the shuttle’s orbit so that it basically intersects the upper atmosphere. The atmosphere does the rest, slowing the spacecraft down. All that kinetic energy (almost as much energy as that of a small nuclear bomb!) is converted into heat, which is why there is a need for some really serious thermal shielding. Returning from a partial descent to orbit would have required another large fuel tank like the one the shuttle used for its initial ascent. In other words, no, that is not possible. And what would have been accomplished by that anyway? The shuttle had limited consumables on board. It had to return. No, what might have saved Columbia was immediate action upon observing the foam impact during ascent. Taking the concerns seriously instead of dismissing their significance. Letting the astronauts know what they face. Authorizing impromptu repairs, even though the probability of success was low. Accelerating the preparations to launch Atlantis, while saving consumables on board Columbia as much as possible, to prolong the mission. All these options were risky of course, but they could have turned a disaster into a success, just as decades prior, the Apollo 13 disaster was turned into a spectacular, historic success by luck, clever engineering and perseverance. Then again, this is all hindsight. What if nothing had happened and Columbia survived re-entry with only minor damage? Nobody would even remember STS-107. It would be a minor footnote somewhere, something to the effect of, “STS-1xx was delayed due to extensive repairs required by Columbia after its left wing was damaged during launch of the STS-107 mission and suffered further damage upon re-entry. Launch procedures were adjusted to reduce the chances of a similar debris impact in future missions.” Sadly, that’s not what happened and seven brave souls were lost, along with a magnificent flying machine. It was eerie to watch images on CNN like the one below. As far as I can recall, these images were broadcast live (courtesy of WFAA I believe), so we CNN viewers already knew that something awful happened, even while NASA engineers were still desperately trying to reach Columbia through backup radio channels. “Columbia, Houston. UHF comm check…”

Are frames of reference in relativity examples of charts on a manifold? Thus, are Lorentz transformations maps between charts? A chart on a manifold is a set of coordinates that covers all, or part, of a manifold. (In fact, a manifold is defined as a point set that can be covered by a finite number of finite-dimensional charts, each consisting of n-tuplets of real numbers.) A frame of reference, in turn, is associated with a specific observer. In special relativity, we can represent an inertial observer’s frame of reference with, e.g., a Cartesian coordinate chart with the observer at its spatial origin. Such a chart would cover the entirety of Minkowski spacetime. However, once we allow for accelerating observers, or worse yet, for the presence of gravitational fields, there is no longer a unique chart that we can associate with the observer. We can, however, associate with the observer a rigid frame of reference (sometimes described by the German word “vierbein” or, more generally, not restricted to four dimensions, “vielbein”) but these rigid frames are “nonholonomic”, which is to say, they do not provide a unique coordinate representation of curved spacetime in the observer’s vicinity. The (global) Lorentz transformation is a transformation between inertial coordinate systems in Minkowski spacetime. This can be generalized to curved spacetime but only as a “local” transformation with the transformation’s parameters varying from point to point.

Can you explain the Planck temperature? And at any point after the commencement of the 'Big Bang', did the temperature of the universe approach or equal the Plank temperature? Can I explain the Planck temperature? Sure. It's a natural unit of temperature that we can use if we measure everything, including temperature, in units such that c = ℏ = G = 1. Of these equalities, c = 1 amounts to measuring time and distance in compatible units (say, 1 second vs. 1 light-second); ℏ = 1 amounts to measuring energy and frequency (inverse time) or wavenumber (inverse length) in compatible units. As for G , however, G = 1 amounts to setting a "natural" unit of energy relative to which everything else can be measured. If we have a natural unit of energy, we also have a corresponding natural unit of temperature, which coincides with a system in which individual degrees of freedom are associated with this energy. How fundamental is this natural unit? No one really knows. Planck units were first proposed more than a century ago by, you guessed it, Planck, but other than offering a "natural" system of units, do they have any physical significance? Many folks believe that our best theory of nature to date, quantum field theory, is only an "effective" theory, and that at the Planck scale, the theory breaks down. Others insist that at the Planck scale, quantum effects of gravitation become important. But these are speculative conjectures, not knowledge. The Planck scale is so many orders of magnitude beyond anything we can test experimentally or through astrophysical observations, we really have no idea how things truly work on that scale. So I suppose I lied. Maybe I cannot really explain the Planck temperature after all. Or the physical significance, if any, of any of the other Planck units. Other than that they serve as a sensible "natural" set of units in which it is easier to write down our equations. Same goes for times “after the commencement of the ‘Big Bang’”. The earliest we can go back to with any reasonable certainty of knowledge is about a picosecond after the ‘Big Bang’. But this time, the universe was many orders of magnitude colder than the Planck temperature. As to what happened before, whether even that picosecond was just a picosecond or an eternity, anyone can speculate, but no one knows. The so-called Planck epoch is much too far beyond what I’d even call “informed speculation”.

Has it ever been considered that the cosmic microwave background at 2.73K is a kind of balance between matter and energy in the universe? I don't find anything googling, so maybe it's a no question? It is indeed not a good question, though, I suspect, at the root of the question lies a misunderstanding of what “matter” and “energy” are in fundamental physics. To wit, “matter” is everything that’s not empty space. All the stuff that there is. In the cosmologist’s view, you are matter, Earth is matter, the Sun is matter, sunlight is matter, electromagnetic fields are matter, the presumed quark-gluon plasma that filled the early universe is matter, etc. As I said, everything that’s not empty space. As to “energy”, there are fundamentally two forms of it. The energy of motion (kinetic energy) is one; the “ability to do work”, i.e., create motion (potential energy) is the other. Motion is a property of matter; potential energy describes the relationship between bits and pieces of matter. The cosmic microwave background is basically a “photon gas” that fills the universe. I.e., a form of matter. This photon gas once interacted with other forms of matter, mostly ionized hydrogen gas and free electrons that filled the early universe. As the universe expanded and cooled, that ionized gas and the free electrons recombined into neutral atoms, forming a gas that is transparent to electromagnetic radiation. Which is to say, the “photon gas” and the (mostly) hydrogen gas that filled the universe were no longer interacting with each other. We can describe this process using our mathematics, and predict the result, in very specific ways as a matter of fact. And then we can compare these results against observation. Here’s a plot from earlier work by yours truly, showing one of the predictions (the so-called angular power spectrum of the CMB) against data from the Planck satellite. The calculation behind this plot involves modeling the various forms of matter (namely, the expanding mostly hydrogen gas, as well as the photon gas) along with their motion and interactions, i.e., energy. But no, not some “balance”; such a thing does not exist. Energy is not balancing matter, it is a property of matter, characterizing its motion and its interactions. At 0 Kelvin, the motion of particles is completely halted. But is there a phase, under some circumstances, where the subatomic particles (electrons) also stop moving? Sigh. You received many answers to this years-old question, but several of them seem united in terms of a key misunderstanding: "particles" are not miniature cannonballs and the classic concept of "motion" does not apply. But first of all, it's important to note that 0 K is not an achievable state. It is a consequence (or if you wish, a particular restatement) of the third law of thermodynamics. Having said that, the meaning of 0 K for a system is that it is in its unique lowest energy or ground state. It is not about motion or the absence of motion, it is about the fact that no lower energy state exists: The system can only receive energy by interacting with other systems, it can no longer transfer energy to those other systems. To elaborate further, think what thermal equilibrium means. You bring two systems into contact, energy flows from the warmer to the colder system until the two have the same temperature. At that point, the transfer of energy ceases. Now a system that is at absolute zero does not have any energy left to transfer to other systems; it can only receive energy from other systems if brought into contact with them. This statement remains valid in both classical and in quantum physics, but the meaning is different. If the world consisted of classical particles, miniature cannonballs, absolute zero would indeed mean that all motion ceases, and the system has no residual potential energy either that could bring parts of it into motion. In the case of quantum systems, the concept of "motion" may lose its meaning completely (atoms are not miniature solar systems with electrons orbiting!) but the basic concept remains the same: Absolute zero means that the system can only receive energy from other systems as it comes into equilibrium with them, it cannot release energy. Lastly, this has nothing to do with the uncertainty principle. Some characterized it as a limitation of our knowledge of particle positions and velocities. That is nonsense. As I said, particles are not miniature cannonballs. Their positions and momenta have no classical analogies. They are described mathematically by “non-commuting” entities, which is to say, their values are not at all like the ordinary number-valued positions that we are used to in the classical world. Sorry, we cannot intuit this. Math is needed. Suffice to say, it means that if one of these quantities, say, the position is momentarily number-valued, the other cannot be number-valued at the same time. The “particle” simply does not HAVE a classically meaningful position and velocity at the same time. But again, while this explains why I stressed the point that quantum particles are not miniature cannonballs, the thermodynamic principles here are equally valid in the classical and the quantum world. Quantum physics is not required to elaborate on the generic concept of a lowest energy state. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Could you surround an object with gravity sensors so small and accurate that you could have an exact 4D map of the object down to the atomic level, with 3 spatial dimensions and 1 time dimension. For example, could you copy a human brain like this? There is no conceivable sensor that would come even close. We are talking about a difference measured in dozens of magnitudes when it comes to what sensors can measure vs. the gravitational field at the atomic level. Having said that, in principle, it would certainly be possible to map an object like that. In fact we’ve done this, sort of. Satellite experiments like GRACE (Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment) have used nothing more than the varying distance between a pair of satellites orbiting the Earth to map the gravitational field of the Earth with exquisite precision, coming up with maps in which the main geographic features of the Earth are recognizable! Unfortunately almost all — scratch that, make it all images that I can find already have the contours of the continents helpfully predrawn, making it hard to discern how much of it we could infer from the observed gravitational anomalies alone. Anyhow, here’s one example: So there, a rather simple “gravity sensor” (again, two satellites connected by a microwave or laser link) mapping the Earth in three, even four (GRACE was able to track changes in the gravitational field over time, e.g., as a result of seasonal ice cover) dimensions. The catch? The ratio of the mass of the Earth vs. the mass of a single proton is a 52-digit number. Do white holes emit Hawking radiation? If no, then would it be the absolute opposite? If so, how would it affect the white hole and space time around it? White holes are theoretical constructs, time-reversed versions of the Schwarzschild (or Kerr) solutions of general relativity. Take the words, “time-reversed”, very seriously. The Schwarzschild solution is not about the object that is the source of gravitation. It is about the gravitational field everywhere surrounding that object, all the way to infinity. In other words, the entire cosmos. So when we say “time reversed”, we are talking about a time-reversed cosmos. Hawking radiation is predicted based on an analysis that places quantum field theory in the curved spacetime background of a gravitating object. Contrary to popularizations, the radiation arises not because of the presence of an event horizon (which, in the case of black holes, remains forever in any outside observer’s future) but because of a past-future asymmetry in an object in a state of perpetual collapse. Now reverse time and see what you get! Incoming radiation. That’s what a white hole does. It absorbs Hawking radiation due to its gravitational vacuum polarization. How can that be? Again, take time-reversed very seriously. Think about this for a moment. You can’t fall into a white hole, right? But wait… a white hole still has attractive gravity! Time-reversed means that something orbiting a white hole would be going backwards compared to what you might see under identical circumstances near a black hole, but when you go backwards around a circle, it’s still a circle. So why can you not fall into a white hole? Because you are not in the white hole in the future. Again, time-reversed. It means causality is thrown out the window, and the future determines the past or the present. Compared to that, the idea that the white hole’s gravitational vacuum polarization somehow causes the rest of the universe to contribute to its “negative” Hawking radiation almost sounds quaint. Oh, did I say that white hole are theoretical constructs? Let me stress that again. Mathematical games, not observed physics. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Is the NASA picture of the M87 black hole credible? 120 AU Schwarzschild radius at 54 million light years distance. It is credible, so long as you clearly understand what you are looking at. First of all, it is not a “NASA picture”. It is a picture produced by an international collaboration of radio astronomy observatories. The collaboration is called the “Event Horizon Telescope”, and they spent several years observing M87* to obtain a sufficient amount of data. The picture was synthesized from these observations. These radio telescopes, far apart, formed effectively a single instrument using a technique called very long baseline interferometry (VLBI). Basically, the radio telescopes received signals from the same source, and these signals were then phase coherently recombined. The recombined signal was than fitted against various source models, including models of the M87 black hole as well as alternatives. The best-fit model wins! With the help of this model, the radio astronomy data was then processed to form an image. The image depicts “light” (radio waves) generated in the vicinity of and behind the black hole, partially obscured by the black hole’s so-called photon sphere. The result is the famous synthesized image, its color chosen for purely artistic reasons. So it is an image that is a result of credible science. But no, it is not a NASA image. Nor is it an actual photograph: the image was synthesized using a very complex set of methods, processing several years’ worth of observations made by a worldwide collaboration of radio telescopes. And there is certainly plenty of room there for knowledgeable criticism of the observations, their interpretations, the models and the methods. Does the problem of quantum gravity only come from the incompatibility of the notion of time between quantum theory and general relativity? Few things appear to be more misunderstood in the popular science literature (and perhaps even professionals who have not spent time working on this very subject) than the issues concerning quantum gravity. Yes, there is an incompatibility between gravity and quantum physics that remains unresolved. But no, it is not quite as fundamental as it is sometimes portrayed. I have here, on my desk, Wald’s Quantum Field Theory in Curved Spacetime and Black Hole Thermodynamics. I also have, right here, Padmanabhan’s Gravitation: Foundations and Frontiers, with an entire section devoted to quantum field theory in curved spacetimes. Or how about the book (OK, this one was on a shelf, not my desk) by Parker and Toms, Quantum Field Theory in Curved Spacetime? As these titles suggest, we do know how to do quantum field theory in the context of general relativity. There are some deeply intriguing consequences, not the least of which is the fact that, as there is no longer a unique Fourier-decomposition of quantum fields (no global family of inertial reference frames), how we decompose a quantum field into particles depends on the reference frame: different observers may see different particle-content! (Unruh radiation is related: accelerated observers see radiation where inertial observers see nothing.) So what is the big deal then, you might ask? What is the incompatibility? Well, the point is, quantum field theory doesn’t simply exist in the curved spacetime of general relativity. The matter it describes should also act as the source of that curved spacetime, i.e., the gravitational field. How? Well, Einstein’s field equations tell us how: G μ ν = 8 π G T μ ν . The G μ ν is the Einstein-tensor of spacetime, the T μ ν is the stress-energy tensor of matter. And therein lies the problem: If matter is represented by quantum fields, that T μ ν becomes ^ T μ ν , i.e., an operator-value quantity, which G μ ν is not. How many apples does it take to make an orange? Yet there is a simple solution. Replace ^ T μ ν with its “average”, its expectation value, ⟨ ^ T μ ν ⟩ . Now we have numbers on both sides of the equation. This is called semiclassical gravity and it works. It works in every conceivable case that we can explore through experiment or astronomical observation. And that is precisely the problem. To go beyond the (inelegant, unsatisfying) semiclassical solution, we need data. We have no data. All we have are competing proposals, but no guidance from Nature. Without guidance, we don’t know which direction to pick: Choices become a matter of personal preference, perhaps even guided by extremely mundane things like research funding. My take is that we will not figure this out until and unless we find some clever way, clever workaround to extract more experimental clues from Nature. And when we do, chances are that we’ll be surprised, and the actual solution will take us in a completely new direction. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Where is the "end" of space/time within the boundaries of our observable Universe if a black hole has an event horizon? Before I answer the question, let me stress a word in the question itself: space/time. Naive visualizations of “spacetime” as something static, an image frozen in a given moment of time, will not do. Spacetime includes all of time, it’s not a snapshot of space at some specific moment of time. So where is the end of spacetime? Well… it’s more like “when”. One “end” of spacetime in the standard cosmological model is that past moment we sometimes call the “Big Bang”: the initial singularity that marks the beginning of time. The standard model cosmology describes space as infinite, without boundary, but it has a finite age. The initial singularity is not part of spacetime. To make sense of it, imagine the mathematical concept of all positive numbers. This set “ends” at zero, but zero itself is not part of it: it is not a positive number. And the set has no other end; no matter how large a number you pick, larger numbers always exist. The same thing with the other “end” of spacetime: it doesn’t have any. The standard model cosmology has an open-ended, eternal future. Black hole event horizons are different animals, but there are also some similarities. For starters, no black hole event horizon exists “now”. That is to say, any black holes forming as a result of gravitational collapse have not completed that process formation, and will not complete it in any amount of finite time as measured by observers outside. No matter how long you wait, the matter forming the black hole might change its mind (or perhaps a previously unknown physical process might kick in) and fly apart, which it can do in principle, because there is no event horizon yet. That event horizon is a forever-future moment in time, not a specific location in space. This is true even if you were unfortunate enough to fall into a black hole; the only difference is that in that case, you would reach the moment in time called the event horizon in a finite amount of time by your own reckoning, and after that, the event horizon will be a past moment in time for you, something to which you cannot return without a time machine. How does Einstein's equation demonstrate the conversion of matter into energy? Can this process be reversed to create more matter than needed? It does not. The famous equation, E = m c 2 (which is not really called Einstein’s equation, but let me put pedantry aside for a moment) is absolutely NOT about any conversion of “matter” into energy. To explain what this equation IS about, first allow me to recall the title of the paper in which this equation (in a slightly modified form) is introduced: “Does the inertia of a body depend upon its energy-content?” (Ist die Trägheit eines Körpers von seinem Energiegehalt abhängig? Annalen der Physik. 18:639, 1905.) The question is answered by the paper in the affirmative, establishing something important: that what we know as the inertia, i.e., the mass (its resistance to acceleration) of a body is, in fact, its energy-content. You add energy to a body (e.g., making it warmer), its inertia increases. You remove energy from a body, its inertia decreases. Notably, the equation is not about converting anything into anything. It is, in fact, called the mass-energy equivalence relation. Which is to say, it expresses recognition of the fact that a body’s mass (its inertia, resistance to acceleration) and its intrinsic energy-content (not to be confused with energy that exists relative to other reference frames, such as the body’s kinetic energy in a moving observer’s reference frame) are really equivalent: they are the same thing. Now about that pedantry bit: The expression, “Einstein’s equation”, is usually used to refer to the equation R μ ν − 1 2 g μ ν R = 8 π G T μ ν , which is Einstein’s (field) equation for gravitation, i.e., the fundamental equation of general relativity. Note that all along, I’ve been silent about the word “matter”. This concept is not even defined in relativity theory. The contribution of matter to the field equations is characterized by the stress-energy-momentum tensor T μ ν , but the theory remains silent about what “matter” really is. This is also true when it comes to E = m c 2 . Presumably a “body” would be made of “matter”, but again, the theory remains silent as to its nature. It only talks about its specific, measurable properties, namely its resistance to acceleration (mass) and changes in its energy-content. The closest thing to “creating” matter happens in particle accelerator experiments, when lighter particles collide with plenty of excess kinetic energy as measured in the reference frame of their common center-of-mass. The collision converts them into new particles, which may be heavier than the progenitors, which is to say that some of that kinetic energy of the collision now becomes the internal energy-content of the collision products. These products are usually short-lived, unstable particles however, so very quickly they decay back into lighter particles, with some (most?) of their energy-content now turning back into the kinetic energy of these decay products. But other than the fact that all along the process, mass-energy is conserved, the equation E = m c 2 has nothing to do with such processes of particle creation and annihilation. What scientific questions need to be answered in order to tackle the understanding of dark matter? Very simple: Direct detection. The existence of dark matter is widely assumed, as we observe gravitational behavior that cannot be explained otherwise within the context of general relativity: the same general relativity that, on other scales (e.g., within the solar system) works with spectacular precision. Now of course just because something works on a size scale measured by light-hours at most does not mean that it will necessarily work equally well on a size scale measured in the thousands or tens of thousands of light-years or more. Which means that there may not be dark matter at all: perhaps the laws of gravitation must be modified! But that proves to be an immensely tricky thing to do, because most modifications run into other observational constraints. Gravitational radiation, arrival times of gravitational and non-gravitational signals from the same event, cosmological observations… the bar is set very high for such modified theories of gravity. But until we have direct confirmation of dark matter, we won’t know for sure. And so far, all we have are null results: None of the attempts to search for dark matter by nongravitational means proved successful. So the jury is still out. Can a massless photon be depicted with kinetic energy since kinetic energy involves mass, yet a photon is massless which diametrically discredits Planck's and Einstein's disjointed theories? Kinetic energy does not necessarily involve mass. For particles that have nonzero rest mass, the expression for kinetic includes their mass. But kinetic energy is a much more general concept, a constant of the motion if you wish, applicable to all systems that are governed by equations that are time translation invariant. And yes, that includes massless photons. In the “disjointed” theory of relativity, of course, time is an observer-dependent concept. Invariance under spacetime translations, however, implies the conservation of a four-dimensional quantity, the so-called four-momentum of the object. Once a specific coordinate system is picked, this four-momentum can be split into an energy term and a three-dimensional conventional momentum term. But this split is, again, observer-dependent. For objects with rest mass, there exists a reference frame in which the object is, well, at rest. In this reference frame, obviously there is no kinetic energy. There is still an energy term, however; it’s the rest mass-energy of the object. In all other reference frames, the energy term is the sum of the rest mass-energy and the kinetic energy of the object. If the object is massless, however, it has no rest mass and no rest frame; the energy term is entirely due to kinetic energy in all reference frames. Assuming you had a long enough cable which connects two people, would they be able to communicate if one was inside a black hole and the other outside? No, they would not, but perhaps its instructive to consider what happens from the perspective of the two participants. First, the person outside the black hole. Keep in mind that from this person’s perspective, the formation of the event horizon remains forever in the future. He would see his friend rapidly disappear from sight, but not because he’s eaten up by the black hole, not yet; rather, because as he gets really close to the black hole, any signal from him will suffer extreme time dilation and as a result, also extreme redshift. So soon enough, no matter how powerfully he transmits, and whether he does so by way of light, radio, or just yanking the cable, everything he does will appear in extreme slow motion, and the frequency (hence the energy) of any signal is redshifted down towards zero. Conversely, any signal sent by the person outside towards his friend falling into the black hole will also slow down and take longer and longer to catch up with the infalling explorer. Soon enough, we see that even signal traveling at the speed of light are too late: They will appear to slow down as viewed by the distant observer, and would simply not catch up with the infalling observer before they hit the horizon. In other words, from the perspective of the outside observer: never. As to the cable itself, what we see is that the tension on the cable increases rapidly. By the time the infalling observer reaches the horizon, the cable would be stretched infinitely, with infinite tension. That of course cannot happen, so at some point, the cable snaps. The stronger the cable, the later that happens but it is inevitable, and it will happen before the infalling observer reaches the horizon in his own reference frame. To sum up: Even though the infalling observer may reach the horizon, that moment in time remains forever in the future for the outside observer; and before that happens, the cable will snap, guaranteed, regardless how strong it is. (But if by some magic — not physics, magic — it didn’t, it’d become infinitely long and as such, unsuitable for signaling as a signal would never arrive at the other end.) Is it true or false that the general theory of relativity predicts light should go straight down into a black hole whereas advanced quantum mechanics predicts that there should be a swirling torrent of gamma rays around a blackhole called a firewall? Not exactly. In general relativity, a black hole is eternal. In fact, to outside observers its formation process takes forever. (The first paper that seriously explored this topic, the famous Oppenheimer-Snyder paper from 1939, is titled “On Continued Gravitational Contraction”). Anything that gets trapped by the formation process, including rays of light, remains trapped forever. Then there is the semiclassical picture, that makes a connection between classical general relativity and quantum field theory. Granted, it does not include a quantized theory of gravitation as no such theory exists (yet?) but it is also not needed. In the vicinity of an astrophysical black hole quantum gravity effects, if any, remain negligible. What the semiclassical picture tells us is that in the vicinity of an object, in a state of “continued contraction”, gravitational vacuum polarization produces outgoing radiation. This outgoing radiation is extremely weak and low in frequency. (The characteristic wavelength is about 20 times the black hole’s Schwarzschild radius.) So it takes an insane number of years (a number with as many as 70 or more digits) for the entire mass-energy of the collapsing object to be converted into radiation. But it’s all there. An outside observer could, in principle, watch an infalling object, never quite reaching the horizon even after that 70-digit number of years, all the while encountering this very weak Hawking radiation. But due to extreme relativistic time dilation, to the infalling object the process may only take seconds! So it encounters the same amount of energy in the form of Hawking radiation, but not as very weak radiation over an insane number of years but as a blast of radiation compressed to mere seconds. [Just to be clear though, the black hole firewall proposal goes beyond this, and proposes a blast of radiation to resolve what is known as the information loss paradox. That is not a subject I wish to touch in this answer, though.] Anyhow, a ray of light still goes down into a black hole, quantum physics or no quantum physics. The main difference is that if Hawking radiation is taken seriously, the black hole is not eternal; its lifespan is finite. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Why does a particle wave exist, and is there a way to comprehend it? I presume this question is about quantum mechanics. In the classical world, we’re used to things working, well, normally. Take a flying cannonball. At any given moment in time, we can describe its position x and we can describe its velocity, or rather, its momentum p (same thing as velocity, for all practical intents and purposes.) The quantities x and p are numbers (maybe sets of numbers, i.e., coordinates or coordinate components, but expressed using numbers nonetheless.) Because they are numbers, we can multiply them in any order: the products p ⋅ x and x ⋅ p represent the same thing. This all makes perfectly good sense, but Nature has this nasty habit of not obeying our expectations when it comes to what we think makes good sense and what does not. As it turns out, things in Nature do not obey this simple arithmetic. Particles are not acting like miniature cannonballs. They do not have positions and momenta. They have states. And to the extent that they exhibit properties that can be interpreted, viewed, measured as positions or momenta under the right circumstances, these can be represented in mathematics by so-called operators like ^ x or ^ p , acting on a state ψ . And these operators do not obey the (commutative) rule of multiplication: ^ p ⋅ ^ x ≠ ^ x ⋅ ^ p . This is the essence of quantum physics. And this has two consequences. First, that state of the quantum system, ψ . It is governed by the famous Schrödinger equation. That equation is a “wave equation”, which is to say, under most circumstances it will give some kind of a periodic solution. So the state of this quantum system will have wave-like behavior, which includes, e.g., constructive and destructive interference, something cannonballs never do. Second, those operators I mentioned, for positions and momenta: Under the right circumstances they yield measurable numbers. So with the right experiment, that quantum system still exhibits behavior that makes it appear like a miniature cannonball. So when you fire, say, an electron, while the electron is en route it does not have a position of a momentum in the classical sense. Its existence is described by the state ψ , its wavefunction. But when it impacts, say, the fluorescent screen of a CRT, that interaction confines it to a well-defined position. Its position operator ^ x , acting on its state, produces a set of coordinates, the location where you see a flash on the screen. If this explanation appears a little abstract, a little hard to make sense of, that is no accident. Quantum physics cannot be intuited. To use a stupid analogy, almost all of us had a chance to play with language models like ChatGPT in the past year or so. Ignoring their more recent attempts to integrate language and visual capabilities, the original language model has no visual experiences. No ability to intuit or visualize anything related to space or geometry. It can still reason about these things, but often it struggles, as its words are not connected to any experience that it would have at its disposal. We humans are in the same situation with quantum physics. Just as language models have no visual cortex, our brains lack a “quantum physics cortex” that would allow us to intuit the quantum world. Therefore, like the language models, we have to resort to painful, slow, step-by-step reasoning, relying on the reasonably precise language of mathematics. However painful this feels, it is important to remember that any attempt to visualize quantum physics using our intuition that is rooted in classical physics is not only doomed to fail, it will likely become an obstacle to understanding. How do you know there is no speed of gravity? For the same reason I know there is no speed of water. I look at a glass of water, and it’s perfectly still. I look at a fast-flowing river, and the water is moving, well, very fast. I look the icy moon Europa of the planet Jupiter, and I see tremendous quantities of water ice moving very, very fast around Jupiter. Or maybe not moving at all if I happened to stand on Europa’s icy surface? So what exactly is the speed of water? On the other hand, I do know, for instance, the speed at which certain influences travel in water. Though it is affected by things such as temperature or salinity, sound travels roughly 1.5 kilometers a second in water. That is true in the glass of water I hold in my hands, it is true in the rivers and oceans, it is even true on Europa. So then, gravity. A static gravitational field has no speed. Why would it? Speed measures change. There is no change when the field is static. However, if you are wondering how fast changes in the gravitational field travel, far from any specific source of gravitation: Why, it’s the same speed at which changes in the electromagnetic field travel, far from any sources (electric charges). It’s called the vacuum speed of light, light being the word we associate with a particular range of frequencies of electromagnetic waves, which also include radio waves, infrared and ultraviolet light, X-rays and gamma rays. Similarly, changes in the gravitational field travel in the form of waves, and far away from sources (masses), those waves are transverse waves traveling at the same vacuum speed of light. But that is not the “speed of gravity” any more than the speed of light is the “speed of electromagnetism”. Forgive the pedantry here, but it is important to convey the correct impression: namely that speed is associated with the rate at which changes travel, the static field itself has no speed associated with it.

Why are black holes called black holes if they are actually white or lighter than the space around them? They are neither white nor lighter than the space around them. In classical general relativity, a black hole is truly black: it absorbs all light that hits it, and emits absolutely nothing. You really cannot get more black than that. Even with Hawking radiation, the situation is similar. Sure, black holes radiate. But astrophysical black holes have Hawking temperatures that are just a tiny, tiny fraction of the temperature of the cosmic microwave background radiation. In other words, even in this case, the black hole is a lot more black than the cosmos: it absorbs many orders of magnitude more radiation than it emits. So that’s why they are called black. Mass and energy are equivalent. Heavy masses dilate time. Could enough energy in a closed container dilate time? If not, why not? I have a feeling reading this question that it was inspired by some kind of (unfortunately fairly common) magical misunderstanding of “energy”. What do you think “energy” is? Is it something that we can scoop out of a container with a ladle? Use it to fill another container to the brim? Not really. By and large, energy can be two things: Potential energy or kinetic energy. Potential energy is associated with how things interact with each other, attracting or repulsing one another. This is the ability to do work: The ability to bring things into motion. Kinetic energy, in turn, is the energy associated with the motion itself. So then, going back to the question: To put “energy” in the box, we need to put things into the box: things that interact (with each other or even with themselves), things that move. And all these things will add to the energy-content of the box. As per the mass-energy equivalence relationship, it means that the box will have more inertia. More mass, in other words. and yes, that also means more gravity. But then, let me get to the second part of the question. Heavy masses dilate time? Not exactly. I know, we say that, I probably said that a few times, lazy language and all, but let’s keep in mind that the theory is called the theory of relativity for a reason: it’s not about what happens to time, it’s about what, for instance, two clocks measure that follow different worldlines between the same two events. I.e., how the two clocks behave relative to one another. And yes, by and large, clocks that spend more time in a gravitational field tend to count fewer ticks, but that’s because their worldlines are, in an abstract sense, “shorter”, not because of anything that might have happened either to the clocks or to time itself. So yes, a heavy box with plenty of energy-content will have more gravity, and as a result, clocks following worldlines that pass near the box may count fewer ticks. As to why that box is heavy, it doesn’t matter. Heavy always means more energy-content. Whether that energy content exists because we put lead in the box, or because we lined the inside of the box with perfect mirrors and then let in a tremendous quantity of light, never to escape… no difference. What matters, as I said, is the energy-content. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Does matter lose mass or energy by creating gravity? Gravity creates energy in the movement of all other matter. Doesn’t this have to be conserved? The law of conservation of energy. Or do we just not understand gravity? Matter does not “create” gravity. Matter interacts with the gravitational field. Anything with energy-momentum interacts with the gravitational field. The potential energy associated with the gravitational field is usually negative. You need to invest energy when you lift something away from a gravitating body. You get that energy back when you let the thing fall. So if we take the energy between two bodies zero when they are far apart with negligible gravitational influence on one another, as they approach each other, they accelerate and energy is extracted from the gravitational field. So the field energy is negative. When astronomical bodies coalesce and form a self-gravitating structure, the negative gravitational energy is balanced by the positive kinetic energy that the bodies gain as they approach each other. Depending on how things unfold, they may remain in motion for a long time; or they may, for instance, collide, with all that kinetic energy turning into a more random form of kinetic energy, heat, which through repeat collisions of particles and the resulting acceleration, becomes electromagnetic radiation (light, heat, etc.) and is emitted into deep space. Or, if the bodies are very heavy and very compact, some of that kinetic energy might even turn into substantial quantities of gravitational radiation! That, too, can carry energy away from the system. Overall, the books remain balanced, as always. Conservation laws prevail. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Why is it so hard to believe WW2 happened for those who didn't live through it, why is WW2 so movie like in many ways? I did not live through WW2, but it is certainly not hard to believe or movie-like for me. I was born in Budapest, nearly 20 years after the war ended. Yet I grew up in a city where, especially in the smaller side streets, the scars of war were still all too readily visible. Damaged facades, bullet holes were everywhere in those old, turn-of-the-century mostly brick-and-mortar apartment buildings. (Many still have the scars in poorer, less well-maintained parts of the city or in spots not readily visible from the outside, such as internal courtyards.) And some historical buildings were still very much in ruins, such as those on historic Castle Hill on the Buda side. Another thing that was not terribly uncommon as I was growing up was the discovery of unexploded ordnance. Radio newscasts telling us that a street, an intersection was temporarily evacuated while bomb disposal teams were on scene neutralizing the threat. Still happens, by the way, though it’s much more of a rarity nowadays. More than that, my Mom lived through the siege of the city as small girl. She has many memories that she shared with me: The air raids that sent the family to the bomb shelter at Christmas, the damaged, looted apartment to which they returned many weeks later, corpses of humans and also horses, the latter sometimes surrounded by people who were carving them up for the meat. My grandmother still lived in that same apartment when I was growing up. She had a container, a large, shiny, repurposed aluminum can that she used to store flour. The can bore English-language markings courtesy of the American Red Cross, part of a post-war aid package to help a starving population. While my Mom and her family were hiding in that shelter, my father, much older, struggled to help his Jewish first wife and child and Jewish business partner with forged documents, which kept them out of the ghetto and ultimately, quite possibly kept them off the trains heading for Auschwitz. He could have been caught, carrying forged, still blank passports for instance when he was once stopped by an Arrow Cross patrol in late 1944. He was lucky: they did not search him. And of course the country I grew up in was at the time still occupied by forces of the USSR, the country that liberated the eastern half of Europe from Nazism, only to install their own version of totalitarianism in its place. So no, although (thankfully) I did not live through WW2, it is definitely not movie-like for me. People I knew, people close to me, but also places, buildings, streets all carried, sometimes still carry, tangible memories of that war.

Can particles moving backwards in time leave a black hole? As far as we know, however, a) actual black holes have a finite lifespan due to Hawking-radiation, and b) tachyons do not exist (which is a Good Thing, otherwise our universe would not be causal, the future could directly impact the past.)

Dumb question of the day: If we compressed a single gram of matter to the point of creating a black hole, would it sink to the Earth's core and eventually absorb the entire planet? What would happen, how would it progress and how long would it take? Well, for starters, even if there was a known method to compress matter in such small quantities to densities far exceeding the density even in the interior of the densest neutron star, it would likely require energy far in excess of the 1 gram rest mass-energy of the matter that we started with. OK, so maybe we can start with 0.1 grams or whatever, so in the end, we create a 1 gram black hole after investing an insane amount of energy by a yet-to-be-discovered process. Well, that black hole would not last very long. It would release all its energy in 0.0000000000000000000000000465 seconds, give or take, mostly in the form of gamma radiation that would be at least ten orders of magnitude more energetic than the particle energies in the Large Hadron Collider. These gamma photons would of course be absorbed by whatever is nearby, resulting in extreme heat and ultimately a thermal explosion with a power comparable to that of the Hiroshima bomb. Kaboom! But suppose we got this all wrong and there is no Hawking radiation; so once created, our 1 gram black hole is eternal. It would indeed fall through the floor and… well, not so much sink as fall freely towards the center of the Earth, interacting only infrequently with the atoms it runs across during its journey. Why? Because it would be insanely, insanely small. Something like 15 orders of magnitude smaller than a proton. And its supposedly enormous gravity? Not that enormous if you think about it unless you get very, very, very close. You’d have to be within less than one tenth of a micron from this black hole to experience 1 g acceleration. Would this 1 gram black hole accrete matter? Yes, it would. I calculated its so-called Bondi accretion rate assuming it’s sinking in a nonrelativistic medium with a density ten times that of water and a speed of sound of 1000 m/s, which is probably not a gross misrepresentation of the Earth’s interior. Long story short, assuming I used my calculator correctly, it would take roughly 10 billion times the present age of the universe… for the 1 g black hole to double in size and become a 2 g black hole.

Everywhere we are surrounded by a lot of visible electromagnetic waves. Why don’t we see a lots of black patterns of destructive interactions of light waves? Actually, you see them all the time. Take a light source, preferably something that has a narrow beam of light. Aim it at a wall. You see a spot of light. Everywhere else on the wall, you see no light. (None from that source anyway.) Now take the wave equations that govern that light as it is emitted by the source and travels through space to arrive at the wall. That wave equation does not vanish outside the light beam. It’s there, everywhere. However, there is no significant constructive interference outside the projected spot of light. Destructive interference prevails. The wall remains dark. How do I know? Say, I wish to solve the wave equations in this case to arrive at a robust, wave-theoretical solution of the projection. Again, the waves are there, everywhere, characterized by a messy integral expression in the mathematical model. That integral usually does not have a neat, clean solution. Rather, I am forced to utilize sensible approximations, for instance the so-called method of stationary phase. The method of stationary phase explicitly picks the light path that corresponds to the strong constructive interference between waves, and discards those paths that are characterized by destructive interference. The result is the calculated spot on the wall. I.e., the method yields the light path that I would calculate using geometric optics, as it tells me precisely where the spot of light will appear. Going beyond either geometric optics or the method of stationary phase, more sophisticated numerical methods might reveal something more than a single spot; the spot may be surrounded by concentric rings of light or similar artifacts, rapidly diminishing in brightness. Here, I have an actual example from work I’ve done in the past. Although this one depicts a case of gravitational lensing, the principles are the same: The image on the left shows an “Einstein cross” (four spots of light) due to a particular (slightly off-axis) gravitational lens, calculated using the method of stationary phase, i.e., geometric optics basically. The image on the right shows the exact same thing, but a more sophisticated numerical integration reveals that there is also light between the spots. In any case, the key message should be clear. The very fact that, despite the fundamental wave nature of light, we see the result of geometric optics everywhere — rays of light, spots of light, shadows, etc., indeed the very fact that our eyes work and can form sharp images — is a result of the combined effects of constructive and destructive interference. In these two images, too, light is everywhere; it’s just that in places where the image appears black, destructive interference won the game. Why would Americans rather drive their car for days than take the train? I live in Ottawa, Canada. I occasionally visit New York City. By car, a comfortable drive with the occasional rest stops takes about 8 hours and that includes crossing the border. It's 12:30 PM right now. If I were to hop into my car at 1 PM, chances are it'd still be daylight when I get out of my car somewhere in Manhattan. Now suppose I take the train. Google Maps tells me that I could depart tomorrow at 6:07 AM and arrive in Montreal at 8:11 AM. Three hours later, I would depart on Amtrak's Adirondack train, which could deliver me at Penn station a mere 11 hours later, at 10:15 PM. OK, how about return? Well, I could board the same Adirondack train the next day at 8:28 AM, heading back to Montreal. I'd arrive at Montreal's Gare Centrale at 8:16 PM. Too bad, that's after the last train that day left for Ottawa, so I'd have to get a hotel room and board the first train next morning at 6:20 AM. I'd arrive back at Ottawa's main railway station at 8:25 AM, just three minutes short of 24 hours since my departure at Penn Station. This does not include the time it takes to get to or from the railway station but it’s thankfully short, as I live not too far from Ottawa’s main railway station. OK, I could take a plane instead. The flight time from YOW to EWR (Newark) is only 90 minutes. Of course I need to be at the airport at least maybe 2 hours early, to go through customs preclearing. And then there is the ride to/from the airport. So I’d have to leave my home at least 3 hours prior to the scheduled departure, and it’d likely take at least an hour and a half to disembark, get my luggage, get a taxi and get from the airport to Manhattan. Overall? At least 6 hours travel time if everything goes according to plan. Granted, it's a little less than the road trip, but not that much less. And far less convenient. What about environmental costs? Google tells me that with Porter Airlines, one flight option only produces 55 kg of CO2 per passenger. But that's not much less* than the CO2 I'd produce burning up less than one full tank of fuel in my Honda Accord. This gets even more pronounced if I don’t travel alone: That 55 kg is per passenger, whereas my Honda’s fuel consumption would not change noticeably just because, say, my beautiful wife joins me for the trip. Would I like to take the train to NYC? Absolutely. And a century ago, I could have. The Ottawa & New York Railway ceased operations in 1957. I could not find a timetable but I doubt travel times were any worse than traveling with VIA Rail and Amtrak these days. Probably quicker and more comfortable, as a matter of fact. But those days are gone. The railroads may have built North America but today, passenger rail service... well, sucks. *Edited: at first I thought the Honda would produce less than 55 kg, but it’s more likely 90-odd kg. Which, incidentally, is just a tad more than the per-passenger CO2 listed by Google for most flights.

If it turned out that white holes don't exist, how would it affect physics? It would confirm something that we think we already know, namely that this universe is reasonable well-behaved and causal. You see, a white hole is a time-reversed black hole. Take the “time reversed” bit seriously. A white hole isn’t a white hole because it repels things. Its gravity is just as attractive as a black hole’s gravity. (A time-reversed orbit is still an orbit, not a hyperbolic escape trajectory.) The reason why things can’t fall into the white hole is because they are not in the white hole in the future. (This is the time reversed version of a similar statement about black holes: Things can’t come out of black holes because they are not in the black hole in the past.) So if a white hole were to exist, it would mean that your own life is determined by your future: You can’t make the decision to fly into a white hole because you are not in the white hole in the future. Sounds illogical? Well, in a sense it is, if we think causality is logical. But white holes don’t care about causality. Their presence literally implies that the future determines the past. So be grateful perhaps that there are no white holes (as far as we know) in this universe. That means that our universe can behave, well, in a manner we consider “logical”, which is to say, causality applies and no effects precede their causes. Does the fact we cannot reconcile relativity or classical mechanics with quantum mechanics suggest we might never be capable of developing a theory of everything? If so, does that imply physics (and science) cannot fully explain the universe? What makes you think that we cannot reconcile classical mechanics with the quantum theory? It is reconciled just fine. The quantum theory builds upon classical mechanics (the Hamiltonian formalism). It refines it by recognizing, as valid states, states of a system that make no sense classically. However, classical mechanics re-emerges just fine in the limit of systems with a very large number of degrees of freedom or, alternatively, in the mathematical exercise of taking the Planck constant to zero. Special relativity is also doing perfectly fine with the quantum theory; quantum field theory, the foundational theory behind the Standard Model of particle physics, is fully relativistic. In fact, we can do quantum field theory even on the curved background of classical general relativity. Where things go awry is when we consider quantum matter as the source of classical gravitation. But here, an important statement is in order. It’s not that we don’t have perfectly sensible schemes to reconcile quantum matter and classical gravitation, either by quantizing gravitation or by taking the “semiclassical” approach of a hybrid theory. The fact that canonical quantization leads to a nonrenormalizable quantum theory of gravity is an issue but again, proposals abound as to how we might be able to overcome this obstacle. No, the real problem is not the lack of ideas. It’s the lack of data. Gravity is extremely, extremely weak. Direct detection of gravitons (assuming they exist) will likely never happen. Indirect detection of quantized effects of gravitation just might be possible, but I would not hold my breath. So here we are, without any real clues from Nature as to which direction to take. So it’s not so much that we cannot develop a theory of everything; rather, it’s that absent tangible clues, we simply don’t know which possible theory of everything to pick!

Why can't an observer just inside a supermassive black hole's event horizon escape if the gravity isn't strong enough at that point to tear him/her apart? First, allow me to challenge your premise. To “tear him apart”, you don’t just need gravity; you need tidal forces, which is to say, differences in gravity. Tides happen because for instance, different parts of the Earth are different distances away from the Moon, therefore lunar gravity acts on them with different strengths. Take this to the extreme, and in the vicinity of a small black hole or a neutron star, the differences become so large, your head and your big toe will want to follow wildly different orbits… thus you get torn apart. Never mind that, you are right, in the case of a very large supermassive black hole, this does not happen. In that case, tidal forces remain weak near the event horizon. But then, it’s not tidal forces that prevent you from escaping. It’s the sheer strength of gravity, not how it varies from point to point. We can measure the force of gravity, in principle, by calculating how powerful your rocket would need to be in order to simply hover. To escape, you obviously need a rocket even more powerful than that. And guess what… at the horizon, you’d need an infinitely powerful rocket simply to hover. Yet… inside the horizon it’s not even this that prevents you from escaping. What this has to do with is not so much the strength of gravity but the nature of that event horizon. You see, so long as you are outside the horizon, the horizon remains forever in the future. At the “present” of any outside observer, the horizon will not have formed yet, no matter how long they wait. The only way for any observer to make the horizon happen is by crossing it. Otherwise, it remains forever an unattainable future moment in time. But once you cross it, something else happens. Now the horizon is part of your past. I repeat, it’s not a place that you can return to. It does not have a shape. It’s a past moment in time. To return to it, to escape, you no longer need a rocket: you now need a time machine. Which, when you think about it, makes perfect sense even from the outside observers’ perspective. Recall I mentioned that for them, the horizon remains forever in the future. So if you were to escape from the black hole, to an outside observer it would imply that you are coming back from that future. There we go again… time machine. To sum up: at the horizon, you need an infinitely powerful rocket just to hover. Beyond the horizon (which is a future moment in time until/unless you cross it, when it becomes part of your past) you would need a time machine to escape.

What effect does gravity have on a photon moving directly away from a massive object? You stumbled upon one of the three “classical tests” of general relativity theory proposed by Einstein when the theory was new. The other two are the anomalous perihelion advance of Mercury and the bending of rays of light by a gravitating body. This one, however, is about redshift. Namely that rays of light, photons, arriving from a “deep gravitational well”, will appear to have lost energy. Key to understanding this is gravitational time dilation: remembering that a “perfect clock” appears to tick more slowly when in a gravitational field, compared to an identical clock that is far from any gravitational source. So then, imagine a ray of light, say, a very blue/violet ray of light with a wavelength of 400 nm leaving the surface of a compact, heavy object. Suppose that the object is so heavy, clocks there appear to tick at a rate that is 2/3rd the rate of a clock in deep space, far from sources of gravitation. That 400 nm light ray corresponds to an electromagnetic field that oscillates 750 trillion times a second (750 THz). That is, 750 trillion oscillations while a clock near the light source counts 1 second. Now imagine someone in deep space detecting this light ray. That person uses his own clock to measure time. and his own clock appears to tick faster. While the clock on the surface of the object counted 1 second, this clock in deep space will have counted 3/2 times 1 second, which is to say, one and a half seconds. So it takes one and a half seconds to receive those 750 trillion oscillations. Which means that in one second, this detector will have seen only 500 trillion oscillations. That is to say, it will have observed that light ray at 500 THz, not 750 THz. The corresponding wavelength, then, is not 400 nm but 600 nm. What started off as very blue light arrives at the detector as light that appears very much more like orange. And this, then, is the effect of gravity on a photon. As it climbs out of the “gravity well”, the photon loses energy, which is to say, its characteristic frequency shifts down, the corresponding wavelength increasing. Do different colors and wavelengths of light have different speeds when traveling through space-time? No, they do not, and this is indeed a very important property of light. The speed of a light ray in the vacuum does not depend on its energy or frequency (i.e., its color). All light rays follow the same “null geodesics” of spacetime, as determined by the gravitational field. This would not be the case if the particles that mediate electromagnetism, photons, were massive. In that case, the photon’s speed would depend on its energy. In a gravitational field, light rays of different color would follow different trajectories. When light rays are deflected by a massive body, such as the Sun, different colors would be deflected by a different angle. We’d see white light split into the colors of the rainbow. We do not see this with gravitational lensing. Not with the Sun, not with distant astrophysical lenses. In fact, gravitational lensing observations are one of the means by which we can establish experimental limits on the maximum mass that photons could have without us noticing. (There are other methods, some even more sensitive.) If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

How do string theory and quantum theory explain light not being able to leave a black hole since light has no mass? Do we need relativity theory to explain this? Neither string theory nor the quantum theory are required for an explanation, and the fact that light has no rest mass (although it has energy-momentum, and is therefore subject to gravitation) is also irrelevant. What matters is that “to leave a black hole” you need to go back in time. Once “inside” the event horizon, that horizon is not a place that you can return to, but a past moment in time. For an observer outside the black hole, the event horizon remains forever in the future. For an observer who crosses the horizon, that event horizon becomes part of their past. So in both cases, “return” involves a) coming back from the far future (from the perspective of the outside observer) or b) going back to a past moment in time (from the perspective of the observer who crossed the horizon). In other words: time travel. You don’t need string theory or the quantum theory to explain why you cannot use a flashlight today to light up a scene yesterday. Not without a time machine anyway.
